topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Shape patterns (age 7+)
topic.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: apply place-value patterns to three-digit operations, use multiplication/division relationships, and exploit shape properties to classify
evidence: Use the structure of place value to explain why adding hundreds only changes the hundreds digit
Use commutativity and the relationship between multiplication and division to derive unknown facts
Classify shapes by their structural properties (number of sides, right angles, parallel lines)
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is multiplying or working with larger numbers, do they use what they know about place value or number relationships to simplify the calculation — like breaking 24 × 3 into 20 × 3 + 4 × 3?

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, using structure extends place value to three digits (adding hundreds changes only the hundreds digit), turns the multiplication/division link into a fact-deriving tool (6×4=24 gives 4×6, 24÷4 and 24÷6), and makes shape classification property-based (sort by number of sides, right angles, parallel lines rather than by look). The teaching aim is a habit: before computing or naming, ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' CCSS MP7 marks this as the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about geometric figures by their structure.
bestPractices: Use a single array to show a whole fact family at once (6 rows of 4) so 6×4, 4×6, 24÷4 and 24÷6 are read off one structure, not learned as four separate facts
Use a three-digit place-value machine / arrow cards and predict-then-check which column moves when adding 100, 10 or 1
Classify shapes with property checklists and overlapping sets (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so classification survives rotation and odd examples
Ask 'which fact that you already know helps here?' to build the transfer habit rather than fresh computation
keyRepresentations: Rectangular array / area model for the multiplication-division fact family
Three-digit place-value apparatus and arrow cards
Property checklists and Venn-style overlapping shape sets
Distributive splits (7×8 as 7×5 + 7×3) shown on a partitioned array
commonMisconceptions: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite knowing 6×4
When adding 100 to a three-digit number, changes the wrong column or mis-carries
Classifies shapes by orientation/appearance (a rotated square becomes a 'diamond'; only a 'pointing-up' triangle is a triangle)
Thinks a derived fact must be checked by counting because facts feel separate rather than connected

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, build the habit of looking for structure before computing or naming: ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' Three strands: (1) read a whole multiplication/division fact family off one array (6×4, 4×6, 24÷4, 24÷6 from the same 6 rows of 4); (2) use three-digit place value so adding 100/10/1 changes only the matching column, barring a carry into the next place; (3) classify shapes by properties (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so the classification survives rotation. This is the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about figures by structure.

activities.title: One array, four facts
feedback: If the child pauses to count or skip-count for the divisions, return to the one array and physically read all four facts from it (rows, columns, sharing, grouping) so the single structure is seen to hold them all; name division as undoing multiplication.
If they treat 24÷4 as unrelated to 6×4, cover a factor on the array they just built and ask 'how many fours are hidden here?' so the quotient is read, not recalculated.
Probe scaling: 'you knew 6×4 — does that also help with 6×8, or 60×4? how?' to check the structural link transfers.
Counterexample check: 'division undoes multiplication — so does 24÷5 come out as neat as 24÷4? why not?' to test understanding beyond the slogan.
activities.rationale: A single manipulable array makes the shared structure of a fact family visible as the child acts, supporting the deriving habit rather than four separately memorised facts; well-chosen representations such as arrays expose structure and can later be faded.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Lay out 24 counters as 6 rows of 4 and state the multiplication it shows (6×4=24).
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn and read it again as 4 rows of 6; say why 6×4 and 4×6 are the same 24 dots seen two ways.
Cover one factor: with 24 shared into 4 rows, read off how many are in each row (6) to get 24÷4; then read 24÷6 the same way.
Say in your own words how knowing 6×4=24 means you already know 24÷4 and 24÷6 without counting.
Try a second fact family (e.g. 5 rows of 3) and derive all four facts from the single array.
activities.intendedInsight: One rectangular array holds a whole fact family; multiplication and division are the same structure read different ways, so a known product gives the related quotients without recomputing.

activities.title: Partition to derive a harder product
feedback: If the parts don't recombine, re-count each sub-array (7×5 and 7×3) separately before adding, and check the split covers all 8 columns with none missing.
Audit the arithmetic together: 35+21=56; if a child suggests another total, recount one part on the array rather than accepting the number.
Ask them to split the same product a second way (e.g. 7×4 + 7×4, where each part is 28 and the total is again 56) and confirm it reaches the same total, reinforcing that the whole is conserved.
activities.rationale: Showing the distributive split on a partitioned array connects the fact-deriving habit to standard structural reasoning named in the practice standards.
sourceClaims: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Take a product you don't know by heart, e.g. 7×8, and lay it as 7 rows of 8.
Split the 8 columns into 5 and 3, drawing a line through the array.
Work out the two easier parts (7×5=35 and 7×3=21) and add them (35+21=56).
State the rule you used: 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3, then try splitting a different product your own way.
activities.intendedInsight: A large product can be built from easier known products by partitioning the array — this is the distributive property seen concretely.

activities.title: Predict which column moves
feedback: If the child names or alters the wrong column when adding 100, predict-then-check on the place-value machine and watch only the hundreds count move.
If a carry occurs (e.g. adding 100 to 970 → 1070), treat it explicitly: the hundreds column fills and rolls into thousands — note this is still the hundreds place acting, not a random digit changing.
Probe directly: 'which digit changes when I add 100 to 470, and which stay the same? why those?'
activities.rationale: Predict-then-check with place-value apparatus makes the column structure something the child reasons about rather than a procedure to copy; such representations expose structure and can be faded.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
learnerActions: Using a three-digit place-value apparatus or arrow cards, build a number such as 253 (or 470).
Before adding, predict out loud which digit will change and which will stay the same when you add 100.
Add one hundred-flat (or spin the +100 wheel) and check: for 253 and 470 only the hundreds count moves, with no carry.

Repeat for +10 and +1, each time predicting first, then stating why only that one column changed (true for 253 or 470; if the column being added to holds a 9, notice that a carry also changes the next place).
activities.intendedInsight: Place value is structured by columns; adding 100 changes only the hundreds, 10 only the tens, and 1 only the ones, unless the addition causes a carry into the next place (e.g. 259+1=260, 295+10=305, 970+100=1070).

activities.title: Classify by properties, not by how it looks
feedback: If the child says a rotated square is a 'diamond' and no longer a square, or that only a point-up triangle is a triangle, run the property checklist while rotating the shape so they see the properties are unchanged by orientation.
If they justify by appearance, ask 'count the sides and right angles — did any change when it tilted?' to redirect to properties.
Include odd and rotated examples deliberately so classification does not depend on a standard pose.
activities.rationale: Property checklists and overlapping sets make classification depend on structure rather than orientation, addressing the common misconception that a rotated square becomes a 'diamond' and is no longer a square; recognising significant structure in figures is the aimed-for habit.
sourceClaims: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Pick a shape and run a property checklist: count the sides, mark the right angles, find any parallel pairs.
Classify it from the checklist (e.g. square: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 2 pairs of parallel sides — also a rectangle).
Rotate the shape 45° and re-run the checklist; confirm the same properties, so the classification does not change.
Sort several shapes into overlapping sets (e.g. 'has a right angle', 'has parallel sides') and place a rotated square and an upside-down triangle correctly.
Justify one classification aloud by citing properties, not orientation.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's class comes from its properties (sides, angles, parallel lines), which stay the same under rotation — a tilted square is still a square; calling it a 'diamond' does not make it a different shape (a square is also a special rhombus).

constraints: The teaching aim is the transfer habit 'which fact that I already know helps here?' — reaching the right numbers is not enough; the child should explain why one fact yields the others.

A fixed reference diagram of a fact family or distributive split can annotate and explain, but cannot be rotated or re-covered by the learner; a manipulable array lets the child test that a turned array re-reads and that covering a factor reveals a quotient. Use static diagrams as support, not as the sole route to the deriving habit.

Matching or derive-the-answer tasks (from 6×4=24, give 24÷6) can check whether facts are treated as connected, but a correct answer may be a recomputed one; always pair with 'which known fact did you use?' to distinguish deriving from recalculating.

Carrying is an exception to 'only one column changes': when adding 100/10/1 causes a carry, the named column fills and rolls into the next place. Address this explicitly rather than teaching 'the other columns never change'.

Fact families and three-digit place value are quantitative; 2D shape classification by property needs the 2D figure and its properties. These do not require 3D models, though a 3D context is not forbidden where genuinely useful.

Optional interaction examples (tap to highlight 6×4, rotate the array to read 4×6, cover a factor to reveal a division, a predict-then-check place-value wheel, live recolouring of a checklist while rotating a shape) make the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general principles rather than proving any specific task was tested.

The original claimed adding 100 'only changes the hundreds digit'; this holds except when a carry occurs. The summary, Activity 3 and the constraints now qualify the generalisation, and the child predicts and checks, so it is not taught as absolute.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Patterns & Sequences
topic.description: Order and arrange combinations of mathematical objects in patterns and sequences
evidence: Continue a repeating pattern of shapes or colours
Describe the rule for a given sequence of objects
Create own patterns and sequences using mathematical objects
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} spot a repeating pattern made of shapes or objects and continue it, or create their own repeating pattern?

pedagogy.summary: Ordering and continuing patterns and sequences develops from duplicating and extending by visual matching to abstracting the UNIT OF REPEAT and identifying the smallest repeating unit — and only these last two mark genuine understanding rather than surface matching (Rittle-Johnson et al. 2013). Teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of repeating units: naming and circling the unit, recreating a pattern with different materials (abstraction, which cannot be done by visual matching), and asking for the smallest arrangement that keeps the pattern.
bestPractices: Shift the focus from 'what comes next' to structure: name and circle the unit of repeat, not just append the next item.
Use abstraction tasks — recreate the same kind of pattern with different materials or colours — which force attention to structure because visual matching won't work.
Ask for the smallest unit ('what is the smallest tower that still keeps the pattern?') to assess unit identification, the hardest and most telling skill.
Include units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC), because children over-rely on alternation; watch for them reverting to AB.
Model 'same, same, different' language and 'start over' framing to make the repeating unit explicit.
keyRepresentations: Colour/shape cube or bead strings
The unit of repeat circled or boxed
ABB / AAB units contrasted with AB
'Same, same, different' labelling of the unit
Number sequences and skip-counting as patterns
commonMisconceptions: Extends a pattern by visually matching and appending the last item, without grasping that there is a repeating unit.
Reverts to a simple AB pattern when the model unit is longer (makes ABAB for an ABB model).
Produces a partially correct pattern — one full unit plus extra items that break the unit.

learn.summary: Patterns and sequences teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of a repeating UNIT. The telling skills are abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest repeating unit — both of which, according to Rittle-Johnson et al. (2013), cannot be done by visual matching alone and so reveal genuine structural understanding rather than surface copying. Build, extend, abstract, and isolate the unit, using units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation.

activities.title: Build, extend, and name the unit of repeat
feedback: If the child only appends the last item without a sense of the unit, label the model with 'same' and 'different' and box the repeating chunk, then rebuild from that unit before extending.
If they produce one full unit then stray cubes that break it, treat this as emerging knowledge, not simply wrong: ask 'where does the pattern start again?' and practise shorter units first.
Prompt: 'Point to the part of the pattern that repeats — where does it start again?'
activities.rationale: Economopoulos (quoted in Rittle-Johnson et al.) argues children must move from seeing a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure as repeating units in order to generalise and predict. Naming and circling the unit makes that structure explicit.
sourceClaims: To generalise and predict, children must move from looking at a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure — seeing that it is made of repeating units (Economopoulos, 1998, quoted in the study).
learnerActions: Continue a given model pattern, e.g. red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue — carry it on further with cubes, beads, or drawn shapes.
Circle or box the part that repeats and say where the pattern 'starts over'.

Name which items are the SAME and which is DIFFERENT: for red, blue, blue the two blues are the same and the red is the different cube that starts the chunk (spoken in order: different, same, same). The plain 'same, same, different' chant maps most cleanly to a two-same-then-different unit such as AAB.
activities.intendedInsight: A repeating pattern is built from a unit that repeats; the pattern is the unit, not just the next item you could add.

activities.title: Abstract the same KIND of pattern onto new materials
feedback: If the child reverts to green-yellow-green-yellow (AB) for an ABB model, lay the new pattern under the model and check unit-for-unit; count how many yellows come before the next green.
If they merely copy surface colours or cannot reproduce the structure on new materials, return to boxing the unit in the model and rebuild from that chunk.
Prompt: 'Is your green-and-yellow pattern the SAME KIND as the red-and-blue one? How can you check?'
activities.rationale: Rittle-Johnson et al. report that abstracting a pattern onto new materials is a harder skill than extending, cannot be done by visual matching, and clearly demonstrates understanding; children commonly revert to AB for longer units, so non-AB models (ABB, AAB) are important.
sourceClaims: Children can often duplicate and extend repeating patterns by visual matching without knowing there is a pattern unit that repeats; abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest unit of repeat are harder skills that cannot be done by visual matching and are the ones that clearly demonstrate understanding. Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
learnerActions: Given a red-blue-blue model, use a different set (e.g. green and yellow cubes) to make 'the same KIND of pattern' — green, yellow, yellow, repeated.
Lay the new pattern directly under the model and check unit-for-unit: count how many yellows come before the next green.
Explain why your new pattern is the same kind even though the colours are different.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the 'same kind' of pattern means reproducing the STRUCTURE (one cube, then two matching cubes, then start over), not the colours — abstraction that colour matching alone cannot accomplish.

activities.title: Shrink to the smallest tower that keeps the pattern
feedback: If the child offers a longer stretch than one unit, ask them to take away cubes one whole unit at a time until only one copy of the unit is left (taking away more would break it). Then check that it still has the full arrangement: for red-blue-blue, the red that starts it and then the two matching blues; for AAB, two matching cubes then a different one; for ABC, three different cubes.
Prompt: 'If I take some cubes away, is it still the same pattern? Why?' and 'What is the smallest tower you could build that still has this pattern?'
Watch for reverting to AB on longer units; if it happens, return to the unit-for-unit check from the abstraction task.
activities.rationale: Rittle-Johnson et al. identify smallest-unit identification as the hardest and most telling patterning skill, not achievable by visual matching. Including units beyond AB counters children's over-reliance on alternation.
sourceClaims: Children can often duplicate and extend repeating patterns by visual matching without knowing there is a pattern unit that repeats; abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest unit of repeat are harder skills that cannot be done by visual matching and are the ones that clearly demonstrate understanding. Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
learnerActions: From a repeating pattern, build the smallest tower that still has the same pattern (for red-blue-blue, the three-cube unit red, blue, blue).
Decide whether removing cubes keeps or breaks the pattern, and explain why.
Try the same with AAB and ABC units, not just AB.
activities.intendedInsight: The smallest arrangement that preserves the pattern IS the unit of repeat; isolating it is the clearest sign of understanding structure.

activities.title: Describe the rule and connect to number sequences
feedback: If the rule given is only 'the next one is blue', press for the whole unit and where it restarts.
If a self-made 'longer' pattern collapses to AB, prompt the unit-for-unit check before they hand it over.
Encourage children to say which items are the same and which are different (for an ABC unit, all three are different), and to use 'start over' language, to make the unit clear.
activities.rationale: The micro-topic requires describing rules and creating patterns. Using 'same/different' and 'start over' language makes the repeating unit clear. Number sequences and skip-counting can be linked as rule-based patterns, but their rule is a repeated step (e.g. add 2), not a repeating unit of items, and this difference should be pointed out.
sourceClaims: To generalise and predict, children must move from looking at a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure — seeing that it is made of repeating units (Economopoulos, 1998, quoted in the study).
learnerActions: Say aloud the rule for a given sequence of objects ('it goes red, then two blues, then starts over').

Look at number sequences and skip-counting as patterns too, but notice the difference: in skip-counting (2, 4, 6, 8, …) the numbers keep growing and do not repeat, but the step does (add 2 each time). Some parts can repeat like a unit, e.g. the last digits when counting in 5s (5, 10, 15, 20 → 5, 0, 5, 0).
Create your own pattern with a chosen unit (ABB, AAB, or ABC) and challenge someone else to find the smallest unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Saying the rule out loud and making your own patterns help children move from 'what comes next' to thinking about the repeating unit. Number sequences such as skip-counting are a different kind of pattern: the numbers grow, and what repeats is the rule or step (e.g. +2), not a unit of items.

constraints: A static pattern with the unit highlighted (e.g. tap to box the unit and reveal which items are same/different) is a useful reference, but a fixed display on its own does not let the child extend, abstract, or isolate the unit; pair it with building/doing tasks.

Sequence and fill-in-the-blank response formats can check 'what comes next' and 'circle the unit', but risk rewarding visual matching; always add an abstraction (new-materials) task and a smallest-unit task to go beyond appending.
Extending a pattern can be achieved by visual matching without understanding; use the abstraction and smallest-unit tasks to distinguish surface copying from structural understanding.
Use units beyond AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation and may revert to AB on longer units.
A partially correct pattern (one full unit plus stray items) is a transitional, emerging state — do not treat it as simply wrong.

The 'same, same, different' chant describes a two-same-then-different unit (AAB); for the ABB example (red, blue, blue) name the two blues as the same and the red as the different start rather than chanting the phrase in order over it.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: swapping to a new colour set for the abstraction task, a 'shrink to the smallest tower' control, laying the new pattern under the model for unit-for-unit comparison, and flagging reversions to AB. These are suggestions, not required mechanisms.

Hands-on construction is central for building and abstracting patterns; conversation can support prompting an explanation of the rule alongside that construction, without being treated as a substitute for it.

topic.name: Linear number sequences
topic.description: Generate and describe linear number sequences, including those with negative and decimal steps; identify the term-to-term rule
evidence: Continue the sequence 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, ... and state the rule as 'add 1.5'
Generate terms of a sequence that crosses zero (e.g. 3, 1, −1, −3, ...)
Describe the term-to-term rule for a given linear sequence and predict the 10th term
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a number sequence like 3, 7, 11, 15… can they describe the rule, continue it, and predict what the 10th number will be?

pedagogy.summary: A linear (arithmetic) number sequence changes by a constant step. The child continues and generates such sequences and states the term-to-term rule precisely — as a starting number and a SIGNED amount ('start at 2.5, add 1.5'; 'start at 5, subtract 2'), not a vague 'goes up/down'. At Year 6 this widens to decimal and fractional steps and to decreasing sequences that pass through zero into negative numbers. It is the concrete foundation for the KS3 position-to-term (nth-term) rule.
bestPractices: Insist the rule names BOTH the starting number and the signed amount, refining 'it goes down' into 'start at 5, subtract 2 each time'
Treat a decreasing sequence as 'adding a negative' each time, the same structure as an increasing one — not a separate kind
Anchor on a horizontal number line with zero in the MIDDLE so continuing past zero is a continued equal step, not a bounce or a stop
Use real below-zero contexts (temperature, sea level, floors below ground) to make negative terms concrete
Include decimal and fractional steps so 'add 1.5' feels as ordinary as 'add 2'
Ask pupils to predict a far term (e.g. the 10th) to motivate looking for structure rather than only counting on
When a wrong term appears, distinguish a slip (miscount) from a misconception (misread rule) by checking the step between every pair
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line with zero central (positives right, negatives left)
The term-to-term '+d / −d' arrow chain drawn under the numbers
A temperature scale / number track for below-zero contexts
A position-vs-term table
commonMisconceptions: States the rule vaguely ('it goes down') without the amount, or gives the amount but not the starting number
Treats a decreasing sequence as a different phenomenon rather than as adding a negative each time; notices only increasing sequences
Believes the sequence 'stops' at zero — doubts that negative numbers exist or that you can go below zero
Reads or writes a negative term wrongly, e.g. −1 written or read as 1 (the raised minus sign not recognised)
Fixates on the last term and imposes a familiar pattern (4, 7, 10, 13, 16 → 18 as 'even numbers') instead of the constant step

learn.summary: Pupils (Year 6, ages 10–11) generate and describe linear (arithmetic) number sequences, stating the term-to-term rule precisely as a signed amount and giving it with the starting number so the sequence can be rebuilt ('start at 2.5, add 1.5'; 'start at 5, subtract 2'), not a vague 'goes up/down'. The work widens to decimal and fractional steps and to decreasing sequences that stride past zero into negative numbers. A decreasing sequence is treated as 'adding a negative each time' — the same single structure as an increasing one — laying the concrete foundation for the KS3 position-to-term (nth-term) rule.

activities.title: Number-line step machine: lay equal hops that stride past zero
feedback: If a pupil halts or stops at 0 ('you can't go below zero'), keep the equal hop going and point to the number line: below-zero numbers are real positions to the left of zero, reached by the same unchanged step.

If the stated rule is vague ('it goes down'), ask 'by how much, and from where?' and test the rule by regenerating the given terms — if it cannot uniquely rebuild them, it is incomplete (many sequences 'go down').

If a continued term loses its minus sign (−1 written or read as 1), stress that the minus sign is part of the number −1 (if your resources use a raised minus for negative numbers, point that out), and place each term to the left of zero on the line.

If a decreasing sequence is continued upward or in the wrong direction, reframe it as 'adding a negative each time' and place an increasing and a decreasing sequence side by side to show the shared structure.
activities.rationale: Setting a start and signed step and laying equal hops makes the constant step felt and makes the zero-crossing a continued equal step rather than a 'bounce' or 'stop'; the 'state the rule' box forces a precise start + signed amount. Decreasing sequences are framed as adding a negative, the same structure as increasing ones, which addresses pupils tending to notice only increasing sequences.
sourceClaims: Decreasing sequences should be seen as formed by adding a negative number each time rather than being a separate kind; vague descriptions like 'it goes up in 2s' should be refined to state the starting number and the amount added each time; pupils tend to notice only additively increasing sequences.
Year 6 pupils should 'generate and describe linear number sequences', and use negative numbers in context and calculate intervals across zero.
learnerActions: On a horizontal number line with zero in the MIDDLE (positives to the right, negatives to the left), set a starting number and a signed step.
Lay each term as an equal-sized hop along the line, one tap/hop at a time: e.g. start 5, step −2, so 5 → 3 → 1.
At the next hop, watch the marker stride the SAME distance straight past zero to −1, then −3, −5, −7 — the step never changed, so the sequence simply continues.
Commit to a rule in a 'state the rule' box in the form 'start at ___, add/subtract ___ each time'; if you type only 'goes down', answer the prompt 'by how much, and from where?'.
Repeat with a decimal preset (start 2.5, add 1.5) and confirm the identical equal hop works for tenths: 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, 7.0, 8.5, 10.0.
Take a 'predict the 10th term' challenge that rewards using the rule/structure rather than counting on one by one.
activities.intendedInsight: A linear sequence has one constant signed step; because the step never changes at zero, the sequence does not stop or bounce — it continues into the negatives. A rule that names BOTH a start and a signed amount uniquely rebuilds the whole sequence, and the same structure covers increasing, decreasing, whole-number and decimal cases.

activities.title: State a rule precise enough to rebuild the sequence
feedback: If the rule drops the amount ('it goes down') or drops the starting number, point out that many sequences fit that description — require the full 'start at ___, add/subtract ___ each time' form.
If the rebuilt terms don't match the given ones, the rule is wrong or incomplete; have the pupil adjust the start or the signed step until regeneration matches exactly.
For the decimal sequence, check 'add 1.5' is applied as one equal step on the tenths rather than mishandled: 5.5 + 1.5 = 7.0, 7.0 + 1.5 = 8.5, 8.5 + 1.5 = 10.0.
activities.rationale: Requiring a rule that uniquely rebuilds the sequence targets the common vagueness ('it goes down') and the dropped-start error, and the decimal case separates pupils whose constant-step idea only survives for whole numbers.
sourceClaims: Decreasing sequences should be seen as formed by adding a negative number each time rather than being a separate kind; vague descriptions like 'it goes up in 2s' should be refined to state the starting number and the amount added each time; pupils tend to notice only additively increasing sequences.
learnerActions: Continue 5, 3, 1, … and give the next four numbers (−1, −3, −5, −7), then state the rule as 'start at 5, subtract 2 each time'.
Continue 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, … and give the next three numbers (7.0, 8.5, 10.0), then state the rule as 'start at 2.5, add 1.5 each time'.
Phrase each rule so clearly that a partner could rebuild the whole sequence from the words alone, without seeing the numbers.
Test your own rule: use only your stated start and signed amount to regenerate the given terms and check they match.
activities.intendedInsight: The term-to-term rule gives the exact signed step; together with the starting number, it pins down the sequence so anyone can reconstruct it from the words alone.

activities.title: Check every step, not just the last term
feedback: If the pupil justifies the next term from a feature of the last number (even/odd, 'looks like…'), redirect them to the step between terms: here every gap is +3, so after 16 comes 19, not 18.
If they land on the right term by a shaky route, have them articulate the +3 step explicitly to distinguish a lucky count from secure structure.
Use the step-by-step check to classify the error: a single off-by-one gap suggests a miscount (slip); a rule based on a surface feature suggests a genuine misconception.
activities.rationale: Documented pupil errors include continuing 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 as 18 by fixating on the last term; checking the step between every pair distinguishes a miscount (slip) from a misread rule (misconception).
sourceClaims: Documented pupil misconceptions: reading a negative number such as −13 as 13 (not recognising it as negative or doubting that negative numbers exist), and continuing a number pattern by fixating on the last term (4, 7, 10, 13, 16 continued as 18 by treating it as 'even numbers') — which may be a mistake (miscount) or a genuine misconception.
learnerActions: Consider 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 continued by someone as 18 'because they look even-ish'. Decide what the next term should be and explain why.
Find the step between EVERY adjacent pair, not just the last two, to confirm the constant step (+3) and the correct next term (19).
Explain to the person why fixating on the surface feature of the last number (its being even/odd) is not the rule.
Decide whether a wrong term is a slip (a miscount) or a misconception (a misread rule) by re-checking the step between each pair.
activities.intendedInsight: A linear sequence is defined by the same step between every pair of terms; the next term follows the step, not a surface pattern noticed in the last number alone.

activities.title: Negative terms in real below-zero contexts
feedback: If a term loses its minus sign, place it to the left of zero and stress that the minus sign is part of the number (contrasting it with a subtraction sign, raised if your resources use that convention).
If the pupil doubts negatives exist, anchor on the temperature/below-ground context where positions below zero are familiar and real.
When calculating intervals across zero, count equal steps through zero rather than restarting the count at zero (e.g. 1 to −3 is four equal steps).
activities.rationale: Real below-zero contexts and a central-zero number line make negative terms concrete and address misreading −13 as 13 and doubting that negatives exist; the curriculum expects use of negative numbers in context and intervals across zero.
sourceClaims: Documented pupil misconceptions: reading a negative number such as −13 as 13 (not recognising it as negative or doubting that negative numbers exist), and continuing a number pattern by fixating on the last term (4, 7, 10, 13, 16 continued as 18 by treating it as 'even numbers') — which may be a mistake (miscount) or a genuine misconception.
Year 6 pupils should 'generate and describe linear number sequences', and use negative numbers in context and calculate intervals across zero.
learnerActions: Read and write negative terms on a temperature scale or a number track that extends below zero (sea level, floors below ground).

Point to −1 versus 1 and say the difference aloud, noting that the minus sign in front of the number marks it as negative (some resources raise this sign to distinguish it from the subtraction operation).
Continue a sequence that crosses zero in context (e.g. temperatures 3, 1, −1, −3, …) and read each term correctly.
Calculate the interval across zero (e.g. from 1 to −3) by counting the equal steps along the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Negative numbers are real positions to the left of zero; a decreasing sequence reaches and passes them by the same equal step, and the sign must be read and written to tell −1 apart from 1.

constraints: The rule must name BOTH the starting number and a SIGNED amount (e.g. 'start at 5, subtract 2 each time'); 'goes up/down' alone is not acceptable because it cannot uniquely rebuild the sequence.
Treat a decreasing sequence as 'adding a negative each time' — the same structure as an increasing one — rather than as a separate kind of sequence.
Use a horizontal number line with zero in the MIDDLE so that continuing past zero is seen as a continued equal step, not a bounce or a stop.
Include decimal and fractional steps so 'add 1.5' is treated as one ordinary equal step, exposing pupils whose constant-step idea only holds for whole numbers.

A static reference poster (worked +1.5 chain, tap-to-reveal rule, zero-crossing example) is useful for consolidation but does not let the child continue their own sequence or experience the equal hop past zero; use it as a reference card, not as the generation task.

Recognition/selection items (fill-in-the-blank continue-the-sequence, slider placement, sequence ordering, multiple-choice rule with an 'add 4 vs subtract 4' distractor) check the skill but recognition alone does not elicit independent production; use them to assess, and pair with open generation to build the skill.

A slider item that asks the pupil to place the next term just past zero (e.g. −1), and a decimal continue-the-sequence step, are useful for catching the 'stops at zero' error and the whole-number-only limitation respectively.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the cited claims support teaching principles, not these specific activities' effectiveness.

Self-audit of arithmetic: decreasing sequence 5, 3, 1 continues −1, −3, −5, −7 (constant step −2) — correct. Decimal sequence 2.5, 4.0, 5.5 continues 7.0, 8.5, 10.0 (constant step +1.5) — correct. Surface-pattern trap 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 has constant step +3, so the correct next term is 19, not 18. The error value 18 appears only as the misconception to be corrected, never as a valid answer. Interval 1 to −3 is four equal steps — correct.

The source for the Year 6 National Curriculum claim is marked verified:false in the row; the curriculum expectation (generate/describe linear sequences, use negatives in context, intervals across zero) is cited but its verification status is unconfirmed here.

The original 'possible'-fit static poster and 'strong'-fit quiz were preserved as scaffold/assessment constraints rather than as the primary generation activity, per their stated limits in the source.

Softened the source's '3D adds no depth' and 'dialogue does not build fluency' framings: these catalog fit ratings are not treated as universal pedagogical laws. A brief 'convince me the sequence doesn't stop at zero' discussion can support the work as a narrow affordance; it is simply not the vehicle for building generation fluency.

Scoped scaffold limit retained from the original 3D 'poor-fit' note: a number line is one-dimensional, so a 3D environment adds no scale or depth relevant to constant-step reasoning here — this is a narrow observation about this topic, not a universal claim that 3D adds nothing to learning.

probeDeeper: Your rule is 'subtract 2'. What comes right after 1 — and how do you know the sequence doesn't stop there?
Read me the numbers you wrote after 1. Is that a 1 or a −1, and what is the difference between them?
Someone carries on 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 as 18 because the numbers look even-ish. What would you say to them?
Give me your rule for the decimal sequence in a way that lets me rebuild the whole thing without ever seeing it.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Number Pattern Relationships
topic.description: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules; identify relationships between corresponding terms; form ordered pairs and graph them on a coordinate plane
evidence: Generate sequences starting at 0 with rules 'add 3' and 'add 6'; observe terms in one are twice the other
Form ordered pairs from corresponding terms and plot them on a coordinate grid
Explain informally why the relationship between the two sequences holds
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} follow two number patterns at once — for example, "add 2" and "add 4" — pair up the matching terms, and plot those pairs as points on a graph?

pedagogy.summary: Given two rules (e.g. 'start at 0, add 3' and 'start at 0, add 6'), the child generates both sequences, lines up CORRESPONDING terms (1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd, …), and notices the relationship between the two is MULTIPLICATIVE: each Rule-B term is twice the corresponding Rule-A term — because the step 6 is twice the step 3 and both start at 0 — not merely 'more'. They form ordered pairs from corresponding terms, plot them in the first quadrant, and see the points fall on a straight line through the origin. It is a deliberate bridge from Grade 4/Year 5 pattern work toward proportional relationships (y = 2x) and functions. Crucially, pupils generate each pattern from a GIVEN rule; they are not required to guess a hidden rule.
bestPractices: Line the two sequences up in a two-row table so pupils compare column-by-column (corresponding terms), not within a single row
Press for a MULTIPLICATIVE description ('twice', '___ times as much') and an explanation of WHY — the step 6 is twice the step 3, and both start at 0
Explicitly contrast additive ('6 more') with multiplicative ('twice') using the corresponding pairs, showing the difference grows while the ratio stays constant
Form ordered pairs as (Rule-A term, Rule-B term), respecting the (x, y) order, and plot in the first quadrant
Notice the points lie on a straight line through the origin and connect this to y = 2x, previewing proportional reasoning
Keep both rules GIVEN — the task is to generate from the rules and then spot the relationship, not to infer a secret rule
Use tape/bar diagrams to make 'twice as much' visible
keyRepresentations: Two-row table of corresponding terms (positions aligned in columns)
The (x, y) ordered-pair notation drawn from corresponding terms
First-quadrant coordinate grid with points on a ray through the origin
Tape / bar diagram showing one quantity as twice the other
commonMisconceptions: Describes the relationship additively ('the second is 6 more') instead of multiplicatively ('twice') — defaulting to additive comparison, which only fits the first pair because the difference actually grows (3, 6, 9, …)
Compares term-to-term WITHIN one sequence (the +3 or +6 step) instead of between the corresponding terms of the two sequences
Reverses the ordered pair, plotting (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), or counting up-then-across
Tries to guess a single hidden rule underlying both sequences rather than generating each from its given rule
Assumes the 'twice' relationship comes from the steps alone, and keeps applying it even when the two sequences do not both start at 0

learn.summary: Pupils (age 10–11) generate two numerical sequences from two GIVEN rules (e.g. 'start at 0, add 3' and 'start at 0, add 6'), line up corresponding terms in a two-row table, and discover the relationship is multiplicative — each Rule-B term is twice the corresponding Rule-A term — because the step 6 is twice the step 3 and both start at 0. They explain why, contrast additive ('6 more') with multiplicative ('twice'), form ordered pairs (x, y) from corresponding terms, and plot them to see the points fall on a straight line through the origin (y = 2x). This bridges earlier pattern work toward proportional reasoning. Both rules are given; pupils are not asked to guess a hidden rule.

activities.title: Generate, align, and compare two sequences
feedback: If a pupil says 'B is 6 more than A', ask them to check a later pair — e.g. position 4, where A=9 and B=18, a gap of 9. The difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows (3, 6, 9, 12…), so 'add 6' is not the relationship; the ×2 ratio, by contrast, stays constant — compare 'how many times' not 'how many more'.

If a pupil compares within one row (the +3 or +6 step), point to a single column (say position 3) and ask: 'what is B here, what is A here, how do they compare?' — the comparison is vertical across the two rows.
If a pupil hunts for a single hidden rule joining both sequences, remind them the rules are GIVEN: generate each sequence directly from its own rule, THEN look for the relationship between them.
Confirm the full reasoning: B is twice A at every corresponding position because 6 = 2×3 and both start at 0.
activities.rationale: Grade 5 pattern work asks pupils to generate two numerical patterns from given rules, examine relationships between corresponding terms, and prepare for proportional relationships. Distinguishing additive comparison (what is added) from multiplicative comparison (what factor multiplies) is a known conceptual hurdle, so explicitly contrasting the growing difference with the constant ratio targets the core discrimination.
sourceClaims: In Grade 5 (5.OA.3) students work with two numerical patterns that can be related, examine the relationships within sequences of ordered pairs and in first-quadrant graphs, and this prepares them for proportional relationships and functions; pupils generate a pattern from a GIVEN rule and are not required to infer or guess the underlying rule.

Additive versus multiplicative comparison (Grade 4): in an additive comparison the question is what amount would be ADDED to one quantity to get the other; in a multiplicative comparison the question is what FACTOR would multiply one to get the other; multiplicative Compare situations must be carefully distinguished from additive Compare problems.

CCSS 5.OA.B.3 canonical example: from 'Add 3' and 'Add 6' starting at 0, students observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other and explain informally why (because 6 is twice 3).
learnerActions: Write out the first six terms of Rule A (start at 0, add 3): 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15
Write out the first six terms of Rule B (start at 0, add 6): 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30
Line the two sequences up in a two-row table so position 1 sits above position 1, position 2 above position 2, and so on
For each column, compare Rule B's term with Rule A's term in the SAME position (vertical comparison across the two rows, not along one row)
State the relationship multiplicatively: 'B is twice (×2) A in every column' and explain why — Rule B adds 6, which is twice the 3 Rule A adds, and both start at 0
Check what happens to the difference between corresponding terms down the columns (6−3=3, 12−6=6, 18−9=9…): it is not constant but grows, while the ×2 ratio stays the same in every column
activities.intendedInsight: The two sequences are related by a constant factor (×2) at corresponding positions. 'B is 6 more' does not describe the relationship, because the difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows (0, 3, 6, 9, …) — so no single 'add a number' rule fits every column. 'B is twice A' holds in every column instead, and here this works because the step 6 is twice 3 and both sequences start at 0.

activities.title: Make ordered pairs and plot them
feedback: If points sit on the wrong side of or below the intended line, check the (x, y) order: the first number moves across (Rule A, x), the second moves up (Rule B, y). Re-plot one pair together — e.g. ask the pupil to point to where (3, 6) goes and say which number moves across and which moves up.
If a pupil plots (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), re-establish the convention and re-plot.
Confirm that all points lie on one straight ray climbing through (0, 0), matching the constant ×2 in the table.
activities.rationale: Forming ordered pairs from corresponding terms and graphing them in the first quadrant is the explicit objective of this standard and the bridge to seeing a proportional relationship as a line through the origin. Respecting (x, y) order is a common error point worth rehearsing in the plotting itself.
sourceClaims: In Grade 5 (5.OA.3) students work with two numerical patterns that can be related, examine the relationships within sequences of ordered pairs and in first-quadrant graphs, and this prepares them for proportional relationships and functions; pupils generate a pattern from a GIVEN rule and are not required to infer or guess the underlying rule.
learnerActions: Turn each column into an ordered pair as (Rule-A term, Rule-B term): (0,0), (3,6), (6,12), (9,18)…
For each pair, use the first number to move ACROSS (x, Rule A) and the second number to move UP (y, Rule B)
Plot the first four pairs in the first quadrant of a coordinate grid
Describe the shape the points make, and notice they lie on a straight line through the origin
Connect this to y = 2x, linking the table, the pairs, and the line as one object
activities.intendedInsight: Corresponding terms of two proportional sequences form ordered pairs whose points lie on a straight line through the origin; the constant ×2 ratio is the same thing as the equation y = 2x and the slope of that ray.

activities.title: Test whether the ×2 depends on the starting number
feedback: If a pupil still says 'twice' after changing the start, work one column numerically: with A starting at 1, position 2 gives A = 4 and B = 6, and 6 is not 2×4 — the ratio is no longer constant.
Draw out the general point: the ×2 held cleanly because the starting numbers fitted it too (both were 0), not just because one step was twice the other.
activities.rationale: A listed misconception is assuming the 'twice' relationship comes from the steps alone and keeping it even when a changed starting number breaks it (e.g. A starting at 1 while B starts at 0). Varying the start deliberately exposes this and deepens understanding of the condition behind the proportional relationship.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.OA.B.3 canonical example: from 'Add 3' and 'Add 6' starting at 0, students observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other and explain informally why (because 6 is twice 3).
learnerActions: Keep Rule B as 'start at 0, add 6' but change Rule A to 'start at 1, add 3' (1, 4, 7, 10, …)
Generate both sequences and line them up by position
Check each column: is B still exactly twice A now?
Explain what broke and why — the clean ×2 relationship relied on the starting numbers as well as the steps (in the original rules, both started at 0), not on the steps alone
activities.intendedInsight: The multiplicative relationship between corresponding terms comes from the steps AND the starting numbers; in the original rules both start at 0. When A starts at 1 but B starts at 0, 'twice' no longer holds in every column even though one step is still twice the other — so pupils should not assume 'twice' from the steps alone.

activities.title: Tape diagram for 'twice as much'
feedback: If a pupil focuses on the extra length (the gap) rather than the number of copies, redirect to 'how many A-tapes make a B-tape?' — the answer stays 2 in every column, while the extra length grows.
Confirm the two-copies structure matches the ×2 in the table and the slope of the line.
activities.rationale: A tape/bar diagram is a standard representation for making multiplicative comparison concrete and is specifically suggested as support for pupils defaulting to additive comparison. It offers a visual route to 'twice' alongside the numerical table.
sourceClaims: Additive versus multiplicative comparison (Grade 4): in an additive comparison the question is what amount would be ADDED to one quantity to get the other; in a multiplicative comparison the question is what FACTOR would multiply one to get the other; multiplicative Compare situations must be carefully distinguished from additive Compare problems.
learnerActions: For a chosen column (e.g. position 3: A = 6, B = 12), draw a tape/bar for the Rule-A term
Draw the Rule-B tape beside it and lay out how many copies of the A tape fit the B tape
Confirm the B tape is exactly two A tapes long, making 'twice as much' visible
Repeat for another column to check the two-copies relationship holds across positions
activities.intendedInsight: 'Twice as much' is a length/quantity relationship that can be seen directly: the larger bar is made of exactly two copies of the smaller, reinforcing multiplicative comparison over additive comparison.

activities.title: Check and sort: additive vs multiplicative, table-to-graph
feedback: If a pupil selects the additive answer ('B is 6 more than A'), return to a later column (e.g. position 4, where A=9 and B=18, a gap of 9) and show the difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows, so 'add 6' does not describe the relationship — whereas ×2 holds in every column.
If a pupil reverses a plotted point, restate: first number across (x), second up (y).
Confirm correct matches by tracing one column from table to ordered pair to point on the line.
activities.rationale: Short checks (fill-in-the-blank, sort, match, plot) verify the skill and surface the common additive misconception ('B is 6 more') and the (y, x) reversal. These confirm mastery rather than build the generate-and-compare reasoning, so they belong after the construction activities.
learnerActions: Complete 'B term = __ × A term' for a given pair of sequences starting at 0
Given a described relationship, sort it as additive ('6 more') or multiplicative ('twice'), and say which one holds in every column
Match a two-row table to its correct straight-line graph
Plot a specified pair (e.g. (3, 6)) on the grid, deliberately avoiding the (6, 3) reversal
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can apply the multiplicative relationship, choose it over the tempting additive description, and coordinate table, pairs, and graph correctly.

constraints: Keep both rules GIVEN; the task is to generate each sequence from its own rule and then find the relationship, not to guess a hidden rule.
Compare CORRESPONDING terms column-by-column (vertical, across the two rows), not term-to-term within a single sequence.

The clean ×2 relationship between corresponding terms depends on the starting numbers as well as the steps: here it works because 6 = 2×3 and both start at 0 (in general, Rule B's start must be twice Rule A's start). Do not present 'twice' as following from the steps alone.

The difference between corresponding terms is not constant — it grows (0, 3, 6, 9, 12…); do not present 'B is 6 more' as a true relationship that holds for a specific early pair. It coincides at most at a single column, and the honest contrast is 'difference grows' versus 'ratio stays ×2'.
Respect (x, y) order when forming and plotting pairs: Rule-A term across (x), Rule-B term up (y).

Recognition and sort/match/fill-in checks confirm the skill but do not, on their own, elicit the independent construction of generating two sequences and coordinating them into pairs and a graph; use them after construction.

A consolidation summary (a two-row table beside a pre-plotted line with the ×2 annotated and facts revealed on tap) can tidily review the result, but a fixed display does not let the learner generate the terms or watch the growing difference against the constant ratio themselves; treat it as a review aid, not the main task.

Optional interactive supports that make the mechanism concrete: taps that fill each row ('add 3' / 'add 6') with corresponding terms locked in columns; a toggle between a '+' view (drawing the growing difference 3, 6, 9…) and a '×' view (showing the constant ×2 in every column); auto-plotting each column as an ordered pair that lands on the ray through the origin; and a 'change the starting number' control to reveal that the ×2 breaks when the starts no longer fit it (e.g. A starts at 1 while B starts at 0), and holds only when B's start is twice A's start. These are illustrative, not required mechanisms.

probeDeeper: You said B is 6 more than A. Check the pair at position 4 — is B still exactly 6 more? What is happening to the gap as you go down?
Why does B come out as twice A — what is it about the two rules that makes that happen?

Point to where (3, 6) goes on the grid, and tell me which number moves you across and which moves you up.
assess.correctAnswer: A: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. B: 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. Each Rule-B term is TWICE (×2) the corresponding Rule-A term, because Rule B adds 6 each step which is twice the 3 that A adds, and both start at 0. Ordered pairs (0,0), (3,6), (6,12), (9,18) plotted give points on a straight line through the origin (y = 2x).

errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up several corresponding pairs and ask 'is the gap the same or growing?'; the ×2 ratio is constant while the difference grows — compare 'how many times' not 'how many more', supported by a tape diagram
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the relationship as an added amount, usually read off the first pair; it fails later because the gap grows (3, 6, 9, 12)

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares WITHIN one sequence (the +3 or +6 step) rather than between the corresponding terms of the two sequences
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to a single column (say position 3): 'what is B here, what is A here, how do they compare?' — the comparison is vertical across the two rows, not horizontal
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer is about how one sequence grows down its own row, not how B relates to A at the same position

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the ordered pair — plots (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), or counts up-then-across
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish the convention: the first number moves you ACROSS (Rule A, x), the second moves you UP (Rule B, y); re-plot one pair together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points sit on the wrong side of / below the intended line; the (x, y) order is not respected

errorPatterns.pattern: Hunts for a single hidden rule connecting both sequences instead of generating each from its given rule
errorPatterns.nextMove: The rules are GIVEN — generate each sequence directly from its own rule, THEN look for the relationship between them; you are not hunting a secret rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Invents a rule or looks for 'the pattern' rather than applying the two rules as given, then comparing

responseLevels.gap: Cannot generate both sequences reliably from the rules, or describes only how one sequence grows; gives no relationship between corresponding terms; pairs and plot are missing or reversed.
responseLevels.full: Generates both, states B is twice A at every corresponding position and explains why from the steps (6 = 2×3, both start at 0), forms correctly ordered pairs, plots them on the ray through the origin, and recognises that the additive gap grows while the ×2 ratio stays constant — transferring to predict the relationship for a new pair or a changed start.
responseLevels.partial: Generates both sequences and lines them up, but describes the relationship additively ('6 more') or only for the first pair, and/or plots pairs mechanically without connecting the constant ×2 to the straight line — has the parts (two sequences, some pairs) but not the multiplicative structure joining them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Use two rules. Rule A: start at 0, add 3. Rule B: start at 0, add 6. Write out the first six numbers of each, lined up underneath one another. Then tell me how a number in Rule B compares with the number in the SAME position in Rule A — and why it works out that way. Finally, turn the first four matching pairs into points and plot them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the multiplicative structure says B is TWICE A in every position and explains it from the steps (6 = 2×3, both start at 0); the ×2 holds in every column. A child comparing additively says 'B is 6 more' — true only for an early pair, and decisively wrong because the DIFFERENCE grows (3, 6, 9, …), so 'plus 6' fails from the second pair on. Whether they compare corresponding terms across the two rows (vertical) or just read a within-row step (+3, +6) exposes the corresponding-terms confusion; and plotting (3,6) versus (6,3) exposes the ordered-pair order.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Generating Sequences
topic.description: Generate terms of a sequence from a term-to-term rule (e.g., 'add 3 each time') or a position-to-term rule (e.g., '2n + 1'), and identify whether a sequence is arithmetic, geometric, or neither
evidence: Continue a sequence given a term-to-term rule involving addition, subtraction, or multiplication
Generate the first five terms from a position-to-term formula such as 3n − 2
Classify sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio), or other
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out the next few terms of a sequence like 5, 8, 11, 14… and explain whether the rule is "add a fixed number each time" or something else?

pedagogy.summary: Generating sequences at KS3 extends the KS2 term-to-term idea to a second, more powerful engine: the position-to-term (nth-term) rule, which gives any term directly from its position. The concept is best taught by contrasting the two rules on the same sequence — term-to-term chains from the previous term, position-to-term substitutes the position number into a formula such as 3n−2 — and by classifying sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or neither by explicitly testing the differences and the ratios.
bestPractices: Generate the same sequence two ways (term-to-term and position-to-term) so pupils see they describe the same numbers, and that position-to-term reaches the 50th term without listing the first 49.
Require pupils to generate a position-to-term rule by substituting n = 1, 2, 3, … , not by treating the formula as a term-to-term instruction.
Classify by writing the successive differences AND the successive ratios underneath: a constant difference means arithmetic, a constant ratio means geometric, neither means 'other'.
Explicitly contrast 'multiples of 3' (3n) with 'increases by 3' (e.g. 3n−2) so pupils see a sequence that increases by 3 need not contain multiples of 3.
Use a varied diet — increasing, decreasing, decimal, geometric and 'neither' — to prevent an only-increasing over-generalisation.
keyRepresentations: Position-to-term table (positions n=1,2,3,4 above; terms below)
Dual display: term-to-term arrows vs position-to-term substitution
Differences row and ratios row written under a sequence
Graph of terms against position (constant difference = constant steepness)
commonMisconceptions: Treating a position-to-term rule as a term-to-term instruction (reading 3n−2 as 'start at 3, subtract 2'), so the first term is wrong.
Classifying by 'it goes up' alone, failing to distinguish arithmetic from geometric or to spot a non-constant difference (1, 4, 9, 16).
Confusing 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3'.
Assuming a later term can be reached by multiplying an earlier one (10th term = 2 × 5th term).

learn.summary: KS3 pupils extend the KS2 term-to-term idea to the position-to-term (nth-term) rule, which gives any term directly from its position. The core moves: generate the SAME sequence two ways (chaining from the previous term vs substituting n=1,2,3,… into a formula like 3n−2); and classify sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or other by explicitly writing the successive differences AND successive ratios. Key pitfalls to address: reading 3n−2 as a term-to-term instruction ('start at 3, subtract 2'), classifying by 'it goes up' alone, and confusing 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3'.

activities.title: Dual-engine generator: the same sequence built two ways
feedback: If a position rule is being applied term-to-term, flag the first-term mismatch: write n=1 explicitly and substitute into 3n−2 to show the first term should be 1 (3×1−2=1), not 3.
When the learner jumps to the 50th term, contrast the instant position-to-term result with the slow term-to-term chain to make the efficiency concrete.
When the coefficient is dragged, show the inter-term step updating live so 'coefficient = common difference' is visible rather than asserted.
activities.rationale: Generating the same sequence two ways and contrasting the cost of reaching a distant term targets the statutory 'generate terms from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule' and is intended to address the misconception of reading a position rule as a term-to-term instruction. A position→term table and live coefficient linking are intended to make the mechanism concrete. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.

The nth term is new learning at KS3; a sequence can be generated by a term-to-term OR a position-to-term rule and pupils should progress from one to the other. Pupils confuse 'multiples of three' with 'numbers which increase by three' (Example 6), and must be taught to attend to the position of a term rather than the term-to-term rule (Example 7b/7c — 'Liam' claims −5, 0, 5, 10, 15 is '5n' because it increases by 5). An arithmetic sequence adds/subtracts a constant amount; the coefficient of n equals the common difference.
learnerActions: Build a sequence term-to-term: set a start value and an operation (e.g. start at 1, add 3) and generate the chain one step at a time.
Build the same sequence position-to-term: type a rule such as 3n−2 and substitute n=1,2,3,4,5 to light up each term under its position.
Switch a sequence between the two modes and confirm the numbers are identical.
Press 'jump to the 50th term': in position-to-term mode the answer for 3n−2 appears at once; in term-to-term mode the machine visibly grinds through the 49 predecessors first.
Drag the coefficient of n in 3n−2 and watch the inter-term step change to match, so the coefficient is seen to equal the common difference.
activities.intendedInsight: A term-to-term rule chains from the previous term; a position-to-term rule substitutes the position number into a formula and so reaches any term (e.g. the 50th) directly without listing the earlier ones. In a linear rule such as 3n−2 (of the form an + b), the coefficient of n equals the common difference.

activities.title: Classify by writing differences AND ratios
feedback: If a learner calls 1, 4, 9, 16 arithmetic, point to its differences 3, 5, 7 — not constant — and to its non-constant ratios, so it is 'other'.
Reveal the differences and ratios rows on demand so the row that stays constant names the type.
If the learner checks only differences, prompt them to also write the ratios before deciding geometric vs other.
When the learner builds their own sequence, ask them to show which row stays constant so the type they claim is evidenced.
activities.rationale: Requiring both a differences row and a ratios row operationalises classification and is intended to counter the 'classify by direction' misconception and the failure to separate arithmetic from geometric. The 1, 4, 9, 16 example makes a changing difference visible on the differences row, and asking for a constructed example practises the production skill named in the assessment.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.
learnerActions: For each sequence, write the row of successive differences and the row of successive ratios underneath it.
Sort sequences into arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or other (neither constant).
Work the worked set: 5, 8, 11, 14 (arithmetic, difference +3); 2, 6, 18, 54 (geometric, ratio ×3); 1, 4, 9, 16 (other — differences 3, 5, 7 not constant, ratios not constant).
State explicitly which row you checked to make each decision, so classification is a test rather than a guess.

Construct your own sequence of a requested type (for example a geometric sequence that starts at 5, with a ratio other than 1) and verify it with the differences and ratios rows. Note that a constant sequence such as 5, 5, 5 has both a constant difference (0) and a constant ratio (1), so it is both arithmetic and geometric.
activities.intendedInsight: A sequence is arithmetic when the successive differences are constant and geometric when the successive ratios are constant; 'it goes up' is not enough, because 1, 4, 9, 16 increases but has a changing difference. The same differences/ratios test can be used to build and check a sequence of a requested type.

activities.title: 'Multiples of 3' versus 'increases by 3'
feedback: If the learner expects 3n−2 to produce multiples of 3, line up 3n and 3n−2 so both increase by 3 but only one hits the multiples.
If they are surprised 1, 4, 7, 10 contains no multiples of 3, confirm the common difference is still +3.
activities.rationale: Side-by-side generation of 3n and 3n−2 targets the specific documented confusion between 'multiples of three' and 'numbers which increase by three'.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; a sequence can be generated by a term-to-term OR a position-to-term rule and pupils should progress from one to the other. Pupils confuse 'multiples of three' with 'numbers which increase by three' (Example 6), and must be taught to attend to the position of a term rather than the term-to-term rule (Example 7b/7c — 'Liam' claims −5, 0, 5, 10, 15 is '5n' because it increases by 5). An arithmetic sequence adds/subtracts a constant amount; the coefficient of n equals the common difference.
learnerActions: Generate 3n (3, 6, 9, 12, …) and 3n−2 (1, 4, 7, 10, …) side by side.
Check each sequence against the 3-times table and record which terms are multiples of 3.
Explain why 1, 4, 7, 10 increases by 3 yet contains no multiples of 3.
activities.intendedInsight: A sequence that increases by 3 need not be the multiples-of-3 sequence; the constant difference (+3) and membership of the 3-times table are different properties.

activities.title: Which rule reaches the 50th term faster, and why? (discussion)
feedback: If a learner claims the 10th term is twice the 5th, have them generate both terms of, say, 3n−2 and compare: 3×5−2=13 and 3×10−2=28, which is not 2×13=26.
Surface the efficiency argument by comparing the work needed for each method to reach term 50.
activities.rationale: A Socratic efficiency discussion can surface why the nth-term rule matters and is intended to address the misconception that later terms are simple multiples of earlier ones. This is a complement to the generator, which demonstrates the efficiency directly.
learnerActions: Discuss with a partner (or a questioning prompt): to find the 50th term of 3n−2, which rule gets you there faster — term-to-term or position-to-term — and why?
Articulate that substitution reaches any term directly while chaining requires all earlier terms.

Challenge the claim '10th term = 2 × 5th term' and test it against an actual arithmetic sequence with a nonzero constant term, such as 3n−2. Then notice that it does happen to hold for 3n, so one example that works does not prove the general claim.
activities.intendedInsight: The position-to-term rule is powerful because it gives any term directly; you cannot in general reach a later term by multiplying an earlier one (doubling the 5th term does not in general give the 10th: it fails for 3n−2, although it happens to work for rules with no constant term, such as 3n).

activities.title: Practice set: generate, fill and match
feedback: Mark substitution errors by checking against n=1,2,3; a wrong first term may flag a term-to-term misreading (e.g. giving 3 as the first term of 3n−2), but it could also be a simple arithmetic slip.
For sorting errors, prompt the learner back to the differences/ratios rows.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, fill-in and matching map cleanly onto the required procedures and give retrieval practice. This set scores answers and supports fluency, but on its own it does not build the two-engines insight, which the generator and discussion are intended to build.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.
learnerActions: Generate the first five terms of a position-to-term rule such as 3n−2 by substitution (fill in the blanks).
Sort a mixed set of sequences into arithmetic / geometric / other.
Match each nth-term rule to the sequence it produces.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency in substituting positions into a rule and in categorising sequences by the correct test.

constraints: Use a varied diet — increasing, decreasing, decimal, geometric and 'neither' sequences — to prevent an only-increasing over-generalisation.
Require pupils to generate a position-to-term rule by substituting n=1,2,3,… , not by treating the formula as a term-to-term instruction.
The practice/quiz set gives retrieval practice and scoring but does not by itself build the position-vs-term-to-term insight; pair it with generation and discussion.
A static side-by-side reference of the two rule types is a useful worked example but cannot recompute for a learner's own rule; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main generative task.
Interaction examples (mode switching, jump-to-50th button, coefficient dragging, live differences/ratios rows) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: For 3n − 2, what is the 10th term — and did you have to write out all ten to get it?
Your sequence 5, 8, 11, 14 — is it arithmetic or geometric, and what exactly did you check to decide?
1, 4, 9, 16 goes up by more each time. Does 'it goes up' make it arithmetic? What is different about it compared with 5, 8, 11, 14?

assess.correctAnswer: 3n−2 gives 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 (substituting n = 1,2,3,4,5). 5, 8, 11, 14 is arithmetic (constant difference +3); 2, 6, 18, 54 is geometric (constant ratio ×3); 1, 4, 9, 16 is neither (differences 3, 5, 7 — not constant; ratios not constant). The child decides by checking the successive differences and the successive ratios.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the position rule as a term-to-term instruction — reads 3n−2 as 'start at 3, subtract 2' and writes 3, 1, −1, … instead of substituting n.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Write n = 1, 2, 3 explicitly and substitute each into 3n−2 under its position; use a position→term table so the formula is read as 'multiply the position by 3, then subtract 2'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The first term is not 1; the terms do not match a substitution check for n = 1, 2, 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies by 'it goes up' alone — calls 1, 4, 9, 16 arithmetic because it increases, or cannot tell geometric from arithmetic.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child write the differences row and the ratios row under each sequence; the row that stays constant names the type, and if neither is constant it is 'other'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts by direction rather than by a constant difference vs a constant ratio; misses that 1, 4, 9, 16 has a changing difference (3, 5, 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3' — expects 3n−2 to produce multiples of 3, or expects any '+3' sequence to be the 3-times table.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Generate 3n (3, 6, 9, …) and 3n−2 (1, 4, 7, …) side by side; both increase by 3 but only one is the multiples sequence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Checks terms against the 3-times table, or is surprised that 1, 4, 7, 10 increases by 3 yet contains no multiples of 3.

responseLevels.gap: Generates 3n−2 wrongly (applies it term-to-term or gets the first term wrong) and sorts sequences by 'goes up/down' without checking a difference or a ratio.
responseLevels.full: Generates by substitution, classifies all three by explicitly testing constant difference against constant ratio, articulates the position-to-term versus term-to-term distinction, and can construct a new sequence of a requested type.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes correctly to generate the five terms and identifies arithmetic by a constant difference, but cannot reliably distinguish geometric (checks difference only, not ratio) or mislabels 1, 4, 9, 16 — has the parts but not the unifying difference-vs-ratio test.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Generate the first five terms of the sequence whose rule is 3n − 2. Then look at these three sequences — 5, 8, 11, 14, …; 2, 6, 18, 54, …; 1, 4, 9, 16, … — and sort each as arithmetic, geometric or neither, showing me how you decide.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Substituting the position numbers into 3n−2 (rather than treating it as a term-to-term instruction) reveals position-to-term fluency; classifying by testing BOTH constant difference and constant ratio (rather than 'it goes up') reveals the arithmetic/geometric structure. A child who conflates the two rule types produces the wrong first term, and a child who classifies by direction alone mis-sorts 1, 4, 9, 16 — so watching what they generate and sort discriminates without asking them to describe the method.

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, 'using structure' means beginning to NOTICE that numbers and shapes are not a heap of separate facts but are related: 3+2 gives the same total as 2+3, a teen number is 'ten and some more', and a bead/shape sequence repeats in a predictable way. The teaching job is not to state these rules but to arrange experiences (paired counter groups, ten-frames, repeating patterns) so the child spots the regularity for themselves and is invited to say what they notice. CCSS MP7 places exactly this at the youngest level: children 'might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more' or 'sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have.'

Use the ten-frame so a teen quantity self-organises into a full ten plus leftovers, making '14 is ten and four' visible rather than a memorised word
Build repeating patterns (red-blue-red-blue) and ask the child to predict and justify what comes next, then break a pattern deliberately and ask what's wrong
Prize noticing over speed: ask 'what do you notice? what stays the same? what changes?' and let the child name the pattern in their own words
