learn.summary: For 5-6 year olds, 'using structure' means beginning to notice that numbers and shapes are related rather than a heap of separate facts: 3+2 totals the same as 2+3, a teen number is 'ten and some more', and a repeating sequence continues predictably. The adult's job is to arrange experiences (paired counter groups, ten-frames, rekenrek/bead strings, repeating patterns) so the child spots the regularity themselves and is invited to say what they notice, rather than being told the rule. For this age, hands-on manipulation where the invariant visibly holds, or the pattern visibly continues, is the main route; labelling tasks and prediction checks are useful scaffolds and light checks, and discussion ('what do you notice?') runs alongside throughout.

activities.title: Flip-the-groups: the total that stays put
feedback: If the child recounts all the counters for 2+3 right after doing 3+2, do not drill commutativity as a rule; keep placing the swapped facts side by side with counters they can physically flip and ask 'what do you notice?' until they spontaneously stop recounting. This noticing matures with exposure.
If the child treats 2+3 as a brand-new problem ('I have to check'), pair the two arrangements so the identical counters are visible, and ask what has actually changed versus stayed the same.
Praise the child for noticing and explaining the invariance, not for reaching 5 quickly — both a child who recounts and one who reuses the answer can reach 5.
activities.rationale: Structure becomes felt when the child acts and sees the total hold steady as the parts move; physically swapping groups makes early commutativity something noticed rather than stated. An optional 'swap' control that glides the bowls past each other while a running total never flinches makes the mechanism concrete.

learnerActions: Drop 3 counters in one bowl and 2 in another; count the running total of 5
Swap the two bowls past each other so it now reads 2+3, and watch the total counter
Say out loud whether it is still 5 and how you know, in your own words
Answer the adult's prompt: 'Is it still five? How do you know?' — aiming for 'same numbers, just swapped round, so I don't need to count again'
activities.intendedInsight: The whole (5) stays fixed while the parts trade places, so swapping the order of an addition cannot change the total — you don't have to recount.

activities.title: The ten hiding inside a teen number
feedback: If the child hears 'fourteen' as one indivisible word and cannot find the ten, return to the ten-frame so the full ten is physically visible inside the teen quantity before re-asking 'how many tens in 14?'
Reinforce that the child saw the ten assemble (one full frame) rather than being told a fact.
activities.rationale: When a teen quantity is placed one per box, ten-frames organise it into a full ten plus leftovers, making the ten inside the number visible. The child filling the first frame and seeing the extras go into the next one is the noticing; an on-screen self-filling frame with the ten snapping full is an optional way to make this concrete. A rekenrek or bead string grouped in fives and tens is an alternative representation that also makes the ten inside a teen number visible.
sourceClaims: Early maths teaching should develop children's understanding of the composition of number and the structure of the number system, and use manipulatives and representations that make structure visible
learnerActions: Place a teen quantity (e.g. 14 counters) one per box into ten-frames: fill the first frame completely, then put the rest into a second frame
Say how many filled the full frame and how many spilled over, e.g. 'ten and four'
Point to where the ten is and where the four are when asked 'Where is the ten hiding? Where are the four?'
activities.intendedInsight: A teen number is 'ten and some more' — 14 is a full ten plus four — not one indivisible word to be memorised.

activities.title: Read the repeating unit, not the last item
feedback: If the child continues a pattern by copying the last item rather than reading the repeating unit, show the broken-pattern example and ask what should be there, directing attention to the whole unit (e.g. red-blue) rather than the single last colour.
Prize justification ('because it goes red then blue then starts again') over a correct next item alone.
activities.rationale: Predicting and justifying the next item, then detecting a deliberate error, surfaces whether the child is reading the repeating unit or just the last item. A light prediction/matching check after the hands-on work can indicate whether the pattern was noticed, though a correct answer alone does not reveal whether the child saw the structure or guessed.
learnerActions: Build or look at a repeating pattern (e.g. red-blue-red-blue, or ABB, ABC) and predict what comes next, saying why
Spot a deliberately broken pattern: 'Is this right? What should be there?' and explain what the repeating unit tells you
Continue the pattern several more steps by reading the whole repeating unit
activities.intendedInsight: A repeating pattern is driven by a repeating unit; predicting the next item means reading that unit, not just copying the last thing you saw.

activities.title: Does swapping always work? Adding versus taking away
feedback: If the child over-extends 'order doesn't matter' to subtraction and says 5 take away 3 equals 3 take away 5, act out the subtraction with real objects (you can't take 5 from a pile of 3) so they see the swap fail, then name that the pattern holds for adding, not taking away.
Treat sensing the difference between adding and taking away as the goal, not reciting a rule.
activities.rationale: A counterexample tuned to this age checks whether the noticing is a robust expectation with limits or a one-off rule being over-applied. Acting out the failing case with objects lets the child see why the swap does not transfer to subtraction.
learnerActions: Decide whether the swapping trick always works for adding, and say how you know
Test it on a subtraction story acted out with objects: try to take 5 sweets from a pile of only 3
Say whether '5 take away 3' is the same as '3 take away 5', and explain the difference you noticed
activities.intendedInsight: The order-swap keeps the total the same for adding, but it does NOT hold for taking away — the pattern has a boundary.

constraints: Do not state the rules (commutativity, 'ten and some more') and ask the child to repeat them; arrange experiences so the child notices and articulates the regularity in their own words.
Do not drill commutativity as a memorised rule when a child recounts; the habit of reusing structure matures with repeated side-by-side exposure.

Tap-to-reveal or labelling tasks ('ten and four' on a filled frame) can show the fact but do not let the child do the swap and watch the total hold, which is where the noticing happens; use them as scaffolds, not the place the concept is learned.

Prediction/matching checks can indicate whether a pattern was noticed but do not reveal whether the child saw the structure or guessed; use them as a light check after hands-on work, not as the primary teaching.
Assess by whether the child RECOUNTS a swapped fact, not merely whether they reach the correct total — both a child who recounts and one who reuses the answer can reach 5.
The swap/invariance claim is scoped to addition (and totals of combined groups); explicitly flag its boundary at subtraction rather than letting it generalise.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Generalising Patterns
topic.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: spot calculation patterns, describe rules for sequences, and predict results using known mathematical facts
evidence: Use a known doubles fact to derive a near-doubles answer (e.g. 6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13)
Notice that subtracting 10 from any two-digit number always reduces the tens digit by 1
Describe a rule for a pattern and use it to extend or predict (e.g. 'each time we add 5, the ones digit alternates between 0 and 5')
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is practising times tables or number patterns, do they spot a shortcut — like "if 6 × 7 = 42, then 6 × 8 must be 48" — and use known facts to work out ones they haven't memorised yet?

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, repeated reasoning turns into deriving and rule-describing: using a known double to get a near-double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 always drops the tens digit by one, and stating a rule for a sequence ('add 5 each time, so the ones digit alternates 0, 5'). The MP8 habit is to notice the repeated step, articulate it as a rule, and use it to predict — while checking it actually holds. Teaching should make the known fact and the derived one adjacent (a double and its near-double side by side) and press for the rule in the child's words, then test it on a fresh case.
bestPractices: Put a doubles fact next to its near-double (6+6 and 6+7) so the '+1' adjustment is seen, not computed from scratch
Ask the child to state the rule ('what's happening each time?') and then test it on the next case to guard against a rule taken from too few examples
Use a hundred square / place-value cards so −10 visibly drops the tens digit each time
Record a sequence and its step so the repeating structure and its rule are both on show ('+5, +5, +5')
keyRepresentations: Doubles and near-doubles on ten-frames / cubes (double + 1)
Hundred square and place-value cards for ±10
Number line marked with equal repeated steps (+5)
Bead strings for repeated addition patterns
commonMisconceptions: Recomputes 6+7 from one, not seeing it as the known double 6+6 plus 1
Applies the near-double adjustment wrongly (adds 2, or doubles the larger number)
States a rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing
Subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones instead of dropping the tens digit

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, this topic builds the habit of looking for and expressing regularity in repeated reasoning (MP8): deriving a near-double from a known double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 from a two-digit number drops the tens digit by one, and stating a sequence rule ('+5 each time starting from 5, so the ones digit alternates 5, 0') — then TESTING that rule on a fresh case rather than trusting it from one or two examples. Core teaching moves: place a known fact adjacent to the derived one so the adjustment is seen not recomputed, press for the rule in the child's own words, and always test the generalisation on a new case.

activities.title: Near-doubles builder: the double plus one
feedback: If the child counts up from 6 (or from 1) rather than referring to 6+6, put 6+6 and 6+7 side by side so the single extra cube is visible, and name 6+7 as 'the double and one more'.
If the child says 6+7=14 (added two) or doubles the 7, use the two rows to show exactly ONE cube was added — steady the adjustment; no need to reteach doubles.
Probe flexibility: 'you used 6+6 to get 6+7 — could you use 7+7 instead (one less than 14)? which double is handiest here?'
activities.rationale: Making the known fact and the derived one physically adjacent lets the '+1' be observed rather than computed, which is the derive-from-known-facts habit the guidance describes and keeps the derivation visible before fading support; repeating the adjustment across 6+7, 6+8 and 7+8 begins the repeated-reasoning shortcut.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
learnerActions: Set out two rows of 6 cubes (or two ten-frames of 6) and confirm the double: 6+6=12.
Add exactly ONE more cube to one row and say the new total: 6+7=13. State it as 'the double I know, and one more'.
Repeat for 6+8 ('two more than the double, so 14') and for another double you know, e.g. 7+7=14 so 7+8=15.
Say aloud which double you used and how many you adjusted by, before giving the total.
activities.intendedInsight: A near-double can be derived from an adjacent known double by adjusting, instead of counting up from one.

activities.title: State a rule, then test it
feedback: If the child announces 'it's add 5' after two terms and won't check, do not simply confirm or correct it — ask 'how could we be sure? test the next one' so the checking habit forms.
If a later term surprises the child, treat the surprise as the lesson: a rule from too few cases can be wrong; revise and re-test.
Ask 'your rule is add 5 — what will the ones digit of the next three terms be? how do you know?' to check the rule predicts, not just describes.
activities.rationale: Recording the sequence and its step together — on a number line or bead string as well as in writing — puts the repeating structure and its rule both on show (representations making the structure visible), and requiring a test on the next case guards against a generalisation drawn from too few examples.
sourceClaims: MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
learnerActions: Lay out the first few terms of a sequence (e.g. 5, 10, 15, 20) and say the repeating step out loud: '+5, +5, +5'. Optionally show the equal +5 jumps on a number line or bead string so the repeating structure is visible.
State the rule in your own words: 'each time we add 5'. Predict the NEXT term before extending.
Predict the ones digit of the next three terms (25, 30, 35) and say why ('they alternate 5, 0, 5').

TEST it: have the adult reveal the next term of the given sequence (e.g. uncover a hidden card or the next group on the bead string) and compare it with your prediction; if it does not match, revise the rule. Extending the sequence yourself with your own rule is not a test.
Then say how you could be sure a rule is right before trusting it.
activities.intendedInsight: A rule guessed from a couple of cases should be tested on fresh cases before we rely on it: a passing test makes us more confident (it does not prove the rule), while one failing case shows the rule needs revising — this is the MP8 discipline of checking a generalisation.

activities.title: Subtracting 10 on a hundred square — and bounding the rule
feedback: If the child subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones, use the hundred square to show the move is one whole row back (straight up on a square with 1 in the top row; straight down on a square numbered from the bottom) — the ones digit does not change.
Counterexample to bound the rule: 'you said take away ten drops the tens digit — does take away ONE do that to 45?' (45−1=44) to check the child limits the rule to −10.
Confirm by reading the place-value cards: the tens card goes down one, the ones card is untouched.
activities.rationale: A hundred square or place-value cards make the −10 move structural rather than counted, and testing whether −1 behaves the same teaches the child to bound a generalisation to its conditions and evaluate reasonableness.
sourceClaims: MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
learnerActions: On a hundred square (or with place-value cards), start at a two-digit number such as 45 and subtract 10; land on 35 and notice the tens digit dropped by one while the ones digit stayed the same.
Repeat from two or three other starting numbers to see the same pattern each time; state the rule: 'take away 10 drops the tens digit by one'.
Test the boundary: does taking away ONE do the same thing? Try 45−1 (which gives 44) and see it does not — so the rule is only for −10.
Say the rule in your own words AND what it does NOT cover.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting 10 from a two-digit number lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — and a good rule is stated with the conditions under which it holds.

activities.title: Check-in: which fact did you use?
feedback: A correct number alone does not show repeated-reasoning insight — follow up with 'which fact did you use?' because a scored blank does not reveal whether the rule was reasoned or guessed.
If the child recomputes from one, redirect to the adjacent known double before accepting the answer.
activities.rationale: Fill-in and sequence-continuation items can confirm a correct answer, but because scoring alone cannot reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned or guessed, pair every item with a 'how did you get it?' question. This is a check, best used after hands-on work; it verifies recall and continuation without by itself eliciting the child's reasoning.
learnerActions: Answer short derivation prompts such as '6+6=12, so 6+7=__' and 'continue the sequence 5, 10, 15, __'.
For each answer, say WHICH known fact or rule you used to get it, not just the number.
Try at least one where you explain how you'd check your answer is reasonable.
activities.intendedInsight: Getting the right number is not enough; the target is reusing a known fact or rule and being able to justify it.

constraints: This is a META/mathematical-thinking topic for ages 6-7: the goal is the derive-and-check habit, not just correct totals. Listen for reuse of a known fact and the adjustment, not just the answer 13.

Fill-in or sequence-continuation checks can show whether a correct answer was produced but cannot by themselves reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned, recalled or guessed; always pair with 'which fact did you use?' and treat them as a follow-up to hands-on building, not a replacement.

A static near-doubles card or annotated −10 column can illustrate the move for reference, but does not let the child adjust the quantity or test a self-stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main task.
Bound the −10 rule explicitly: it lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — this specific 'drop the tens by one' rule does not generalise to −1 or other amounts.
Do not confirm or correct a child's sequence rule for them when the aim is building the checking habit; prompt them to test the next case instead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original recommendation leaned on a specific interactive 'near-doubles builder' and 'sequence machine' and rated conversation and 3D artefacts 'poor'. Those comparative/necessity ratings are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; the concrete affordances (live total update when a cube is added, a machine flagging a wrong predicted term) are preserved here as optional ways to make the mechanism visible, achievable with physical cubes, ten-frames, number lines, bead strings, hundred squares, or screen tools.

The original claims that '3D adds no structural information' and that 'open dialogue gives nothing concrete' were omitted as unsupported universal statements; spoken explanation of which fact was used is in fact central to assessing this reasoning habit, while a sort or fill-in check alone verifies classification/recall without eliciting that explanation.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, repeated reasoning matures into working the multiplication tables as a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns: noticing all multiples of 4 are even and using that to CHECK an answer, deriving 8×7 from 8×5 + 8×2, and describing the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward. The MP8 emphasis on 'maintaining oversight… evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results' becomes concrete here: a pattern (multiples of 4 are even) is not just noticed but used as a reasonableness check. Teaching should build tables from known facts and pattern, not rote alone, and always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'
bestPractices: Derive harder table facts from anchor facts (×5 and ×2 to reach ×7) using an array split, so the table is a network not a list to memorise
Explicitly use pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is your answer even?' to build reasonableness monitoring
Have children describe the rule of a growing sequence and predict several terms ahead, then verify

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, turn multiplication tables from a memorised list into a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns. Children derive a harder fact (8×7) from anchor facts they own (8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56) using an array split, use a pattern as a reasonableness check (multiples of 4 and 8 are even — is my answer even?), and describe/test the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward terms. The core habit is deriving AND self-checking, plus probing what a pattern does and does not claim.

activities.title: Split an array to derive a hard fact
feedback: If a child skip-counts 8, 16, 24… or recalls insecurely: show the array split into 8×5 and 8×2 so the two anchor facts are visible to combine.
If a child computes 8×5 + 2 = 42 (forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8): return to the array — the second block is also 8 tall, so it is 8×2 = 16, not 2. This is a scaffolding nudge, not a full reteach.
Correct target: 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56 (and equivalently 8×8 − 8 = 56).
activities.rationale: Deriving facts from known facts and using arrays that reveal structure supports reasoning over rote recall; a splittable/foldable array makes the decomposition something the child acts on.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Face 8×7 shown as an array 8 rows tall and 7 wide.
Cut the 7 into 5 and 2 (drag a divider, fold a paper array, or draw a line) so the array cleaves into an 8×5 block and an 8×2 block.
Read off 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then combine the two blocks to get 56.

Try a different way to reach the same answer: 8×8 − 8 = 64 − 8 = 56 (take one group of 8 away from eight 8s). Compare which way you prefer and why — this uses one fewer group of 8, which is a different idea from cutting the 7 into 5 and 2.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'hard' table fact can be assembled from facts you already own; the array makes the decomposition (distributive idea) visible rather than relying on recall or skip-counting, and the 8×8 − 8 route is a distinct alternative strategy (adjusting from a near fact), not another split of the 7.

activities.title: Use a table pattern as a reasonableness check
feedback: If a child has no test when asked to check: practise 'multiples of 4/8 are even; is yours?' and connect it back to the shaded grid.

If a child accepts an odd number as a multiple of 4: point to the shaded multiples of 4 (a single column or row on a multiplication grid, a staggered pattern on a 10-wide hundred square) — no odd number is shaded.
A product that is odd cannot be a multiple of 4 or 8; a product well outside the 40–64 range for 8×7 should prompt a recheck — then confirm the exact value by the derivation.
activities.rationale: Maintaining oversight by evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results is central to MP8; a shadeable grid makes the pattern visible so it can be used as a live check.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Shade the multiples of 4 (and of 8) on a multiplication grid or hundred square and observe that every one is even.
State the pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is my answer even?'
Apply the check to a proposed product: given a candidate like an odd 'multiple of 4', decide whether it can be right and say why.
Estimate before computing: 'roughly how big should 8×7 be — between which two facts I know?' (between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64).
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed pattern is not just an observation — it becomes a tool you use to catch your own errors and judge whether an answer looks plausible (this check shows an answer is plausible, e.g. even and within range, not that it is exactly right).

activities.title: Describe and test a sequence rule
feedback: If a child only continues one step: ask them to state the rule explicitly first, then jump ahead using it.
Check predictions against equal repeated steps on the number line; a term that breaks the constant step signals an arithmetic slip.
activities.rationale: Describing the regularity in repeated reasoning and using it to predict, then checking, is the sequence form of MP8.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
learnerActions: Given a growing sequence (e.g. steps of +50 along a number line), describe the rule in words: 'add 50 each time'.
Predict several terms ahead — e.g. the term after 350 (400), and the one after that (450) — then verify by stepping along the number line.
Say how sure you are and how you could check a predicted term.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly stated rule lets you predict beyond what you can see and then verify, which is the predict-and-check habit in a sequence context.

activities.title: Test the limits of a pattern (don't over-reverse it)
feedback: If a child says 18 (or 6) is a multiple of 4 because it is even: offer the counterexample and ask them to list actual multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, 16…) to see 6 and 18 are absent.
Correct distinction: 'multiple of 4 ⇒ even' holds, but 'even ⇒ multiple of 4' is false.
activities.rationale: Surfacing and testing near-generalisations guards against over-generalising a pattern from a few cases or reversing it wrongly; this is recognising precisely what the mathematical structure does and does not entail.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'all multiples of 4 are even' and agree it is true.
Now test the reverse: 'is every even number a multiple of 4?' Try 6 — it is even but not a multiple of 4.
State precisely what the rule claims and what it does not (every multiple of 4 is even, but not every even number is a multiple of 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A true pattern often does not reverse; testing a near-generalisation with a counterexample sharpens exactly what a rule does and doesn't claim.

activities.title: Check understanding with targeted questions
feedback: Include an '8×5 + 2' distractor for the split: the correct combination is 8×5 + 8×2, so the second term is 16, not 2 (giving 56, not 42).
For the sorting task, an even number that is not a multiple of 4 (like 6) tests whether the child over-reverses the pattern.
Pair each selection with a 'why' so recognition is backed by reasoning, not guessing.
activities.rationale: At this age, well-designed questions can probe the derivation and reasonableness-checking content when paired with a justification step; note this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not independent construction, so pair it with open construction tasks.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
learnerActions: Answer 'which known facts can you combine to make 8×7?' and explain why your choice works.
Sort a set of numbers into multiples of 4 and not-multiples-of-4, including an even non-multiple to catch over-generalising.
Spot the unreasonable answer: given candidate products, identify one that breaks a pattern (e.g. an odd 'multiple of 8') and say which pattern it breaks.
activities.intendedInsight: Questions can check both the derivation route and the pattern-as-check habit, including whether a child is fooled by a plausible wrong split; this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not whether the child can construct the derivation unprompted.

constraints: Build tables from known facts and visible pattern, not rote memorisation alone; always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'

Arrays and grids should be things the child acts on (cut, fold, shade) so the derivation and pattern are visible; a pre-split array or fixed shaded grid with tap-to-reveal annotations can illustrate and reference the method but does not let the child choose the split or test their own candidate answer against the pattern — treat it as a scaffold.

Recognition/selection questions check whether a child can identify a correct split or sort numbers, but do not by themselves require the child to construct a derivation unprompted; pair with a spoken or written 'why' and with open construction tasks.
Open discussion alone supplies nothing to split or shade; pair talk with an array, grid, or number line (a practical pairing, not a claim that talk cannot support reasoning).
These are flat number-and-pattern ideas; a 3D presentation is not needed and may add load — this is a practical note for this topic, not a universal claim about 3D.
Pattern-as-check establishes that an answer is plausible (e.g. even, within a range), not that it is exactly correct; keep both the derivation and the check.
Keep the 8×5 + 8×2 array split distinct from the 8×8 − 8 near-fact route; both reach 56 but they are different strategies (decomposition vs. adjusting from a known neighbour).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 8×5=40, 8×2=16, 40+16=56; alternative 8×8−8 = 64−8 = 56; both confirmed. Estimation bound 'between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64' is correct for 8×7=56. Sequence +50 from 350 gives 400 then 450.

Self-audit (pattern logic): 'all multiples of 4 are even' is true; its reverse is false (6 and 18 are even but not multiples of 4); 18 is not a multiple of 4. The '8×5 + 2 = 42' error is a genuine common slip and is used only as a diagnosed misconception, never offered as a correct option.

The original claims that 'open talk supplies nothing' and '3D adds load, not insight' were softened to scoped practical notes; catalog fit rankings are not evidence of comparative efficacy or necessity.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Generalising with repeated reasoning
topic.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: describe algebraic rules for nth terms, use properties of operations to simplify, and verify generalisations with specific cases
evidence: Explain that the interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2) × 180° based on the pattern for triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons
Predict the 20th term of a linear sequence by identifying and applying the general rule
Generalise that dividing by n always gives a denominator of n in the fraction, for any whole numbers
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} finds the rule for a number sequence — like "add 7 each time" or "multiply the position number by 3" — can they use that rule to find any term without having to list all the ones before it?

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 this is the capstone of repeated reasoning: abstracting an algebraic rule from a run of cases and VERIFYING it. The child builds the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, writes the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalises structural facts — always testing the generalisation on a specific case. CCSS MP8's own high examples live here: abstracting slope into (y−2)/(x−1)=3, and spotting the cancelling pattern in (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula. Teaching should organise cases in a table so the regularity is visible, press for the general rule in symbols, and demand a verifying case — the difference between a conjecture and a checked generalisation.
bestPractices: Tabulate a family of cases (polygon sides vs angle sum; position vs term) so the constant step and the offset are visible before the rule is written
Move from 'what's the pattern?' to 'write the rule for the nth/any case' in words then symbols
Always verify a stated generalisation on a fresh specific case (test (n−2)×180 on a hexagon) before trusting it
Decompose the geometric case (split a polygon into n−2 triangles) so the rule is explained, not just fitted
keyRepresentations: Polygon triangulation (an n-gon splits into n−2 triangles)
Position-vs-term tables and the nth-term expression
Linear-sequence graphs/number lines showing constant difference and offset
Algebra tiles / area models for operation-property generalisations
commonMisconceptions: Uses a term-to-term rule and cannot produce an nth-term rule for a far term
Assumes direct proportion — e.g. angle sum is n×180° or the 20th term is 20×(first term) — ignoring the −2 offset / start value
States a generalisation but never verifies it on a specific case, so errors go uncaught
Fits a rule to the given cases that fails to generalise (a pattern that works for 3, 4, 5 sides but wasn't reasoned from structure)

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, this is the capstone of 'look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning': abstract a general algebraic rule from a run of specific cases AND verify it on a fresh case. Learners build the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, write the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalise structural facts about operations — each time testing the generalisation on a specific case. The core discrimination is twofold: (a) capturing the −2 offset / start value instead of assuming direct proportion (n×180°, or 20th term = 20×first term), and (b) treating verification on a new case as a reflex, not an afterthought. Teaching should tabulate the cases so the constant step and offset are visible, press for the rule in words then symbols, decompose the geometric case so the rule is explained rather than curve-fitted, and always demand a verifying case.

activities.title: Polygon angle-sum explorer: build, tabulate, abstract, verify
feedback: If the learner writes n×180° (e.g. 6×180 = 1080° for a hexagon), triangulate the hexagon together and count: there are 4 triangles, not 6. Test the n×180 rule against the known pentagon (it gives 900°, not 540°) and watch it fail — a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex always yields exactly n−2 triangles, so the sum is (n−2) lots of 180°, not n.

If the learner states a rule and stops, do not confirm it; ask 'does it give the pentagon's 540°? Now test the hexagon, which you held back and did not use to build the rule.' Make the verifying case a required step every time.
If the learner reaches (n−2)×180° with the triangle reasoning and checks the hexagon at 720°, affirm both the structural justification AND the check as the target — the formula alone is not enough.
activities.rationale: Tabulating a family of cases makes the constant step (+180°) and the offset (−2) visible before the rule is written; decomposing the polygon into n−2 triangles explains the rule structurally so it generalises instead of merely fitting 3,4,5 sides; demanding a fresh verifying case separates a conjecture from a checked generalisation.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Start with a triangle (angle sum 180°). Add one side at a time to make a quadrilateral, then a pentagon (convex shapes); for each, split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Keep the hexagon back as a fresh test case.
Record in a running table: number of sides, number of triangles, and angle sum. Notice the sum climbs by a steady +180° each time while the triangle count stays at (sides − 2).

Explain WHY: in a convex polygon, from one vertex you can reach the n−3 non-adjacent vertices by diagonals, so an n-sided polygon splits into exactly n−2 triangles, and its angle sum is (n−2) lots of 180° — reason the rule from the structure, don't just fit it to the numbers.
Write the general rule in words ('two fewer than the number of sides, times 180°') then in symbols: (n−2)×180°.

Verify on a case you did not build the rule from: test a hexagon — (6−2)×180° = 720° — and check it matches the measured/added angles. Then stretch it: a decagon (10 sides, 1440°) and a 100-gon — does it still make sense?
activities.intendedInsight: The angle sum is (n−2)×180° BECAUSE the polygon decomposes into n−2 triangles — a rule explained by structure, and confirmed by testing a new polygon rather than trusted on faith.

activities.title: nth-term rule tester for a linear sequence
feedback: If the learner extends the sequence step by step instead of writing a rule, tabulate position against term and ask for the 100th term — continuing by hand becomes impractical, motivating the nth-term rule.

If the learner writes 20 × (first term) for the 20th term, test that rule against a known term (does term = position × first term give the 2nd term correctly? 2×5 = 10, but the 2nd term is 9) and see it fail; locate the missing offset.

If the learner writes 4n + 1, checks it against the listed terms and then confirms it on a fresh term such as the 5th (21), affirm that testing a case not used to build the rule is how you move from a conjecture to a checked generalisation.
activities.rationale: Position-vs-term tables reveal the difference and offset; requiring prediction of a far term forces a genuine nth-term rule rather than term-to-term iteration; checking the rule against a listed term builds verification into the habit and exposes the direct-proportion misconception.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Take a linear sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and tabulate position (1, 2, 3, 4) against term so the constant difference (+4) and the start value are visible.
Move from the term-to-term rule ('add 4') to a position-to-term rule: difference × n + offset. For 5, 9, 13, 17 this is 4n + 1.
Predict a far term you cannot easily count to — the 20th term (81) and the 100th term (401) — using the rule, not step-by-step continuation.

Verify: first check your rule reproduces every listed term (e.g. the 4th term should give 4×4+1 = 17), then test a fresh case not used to build it — extend the sequence by one step to get the 5th term (21) and check that 4×5+1 = 21. If a conjectured rule breaks any term, it is wrong — fix it.
Explain why direct proportion fails here: the 20th term is NOT 20 × the first term, because the sequence does not pass through zero at position zero (the rule 4n+1 gives 1 at n=0, not 0).
activities.intendedInsight: A general nth-term rule lets you jump to any term directly, and the offset (start value) matters — direct proportion from the first term is a classic error that verification against a known term catches.

activities.title: Generalise a structural fact and find the case that disproves a false rule
feedback: If a learner cannot say what the −2 corresponds to, return to the triangulation of a convex polygon: from one vertex you can draw diagonals only to the n−3 non-adjacent vertices, which splits the polygon into exactly n−2 triangles (a hexagon gives 4). Each side not touching the chosen vertex is the base of one triangle; the 2 sides that meet at the chosen vertex do not get a triangle of their own, which is where the −2 comes from.
If a learner accepts a false rule, ask them to find one polygon (or one sequence term) where it breaks; a single counterexample is enough to reject it.
Affirm a response that states the rule, grounds it in structure, and can name a disproving case for a false alternative.
activities.rationale: Reasoning about why a relationship holds (not just that it fits cases) is what makes a generalisation reliable; practising counterexample selection trains the verification habit the assessment targets. Algebra tiles/area models are offered as optional representations that may make the structure visible for simpler products.
sourceClaims: MP8's advanced examples: abstracting slope into an equation from repeated checks, and noticing the cancelling regularity across (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula — generalising from repeated reasoning
Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Generalise an operation property with a reason, e.g. 'any whole number m divided by a non-zero whole number n can be written as the fraction m/n, so dividing by n gives a denominator of n (before any simplifying)' — state it, then justify why it holds, not just that it works on examples.

Explore the cancelling regularity in products like (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1), … and describe the general pattern that emerges; an area model or algebra tiles may help visualise the simpler binomial product (x−1)(x+1), but are harder to apply to the cubic case, so treat them as an optional aid rather than a required method.

Practise verification-by-counterexample: given a false claim such as 'a polygon's angle sum is n×180°', name the specific polygon that shows it is wrong and state what it gives versus the true value (e.g. pentagon: rule gives 900°, truth is 540°).
Answer the discriminating prompt: 'Why n−2 and not n — what does the −2 correspond to in the shape?'
activities.intendedInsight: Generalising means stating a rule, justifying why it holds from structure, and being able to produce the single case that would disprove a false version — all three are part of mathematical reasoning.

constraints: Verification is not optional: every stated generalisation must be tested on a fresh specific case before it is trusted. Do not let a learner stop at a rule, and do not simply confirm a rule for them — ask for the verifying case.
Guard against the direct-proportion misconception explicitly: n×180° for angle sums and 20×(first term) for the 20th term are the key errors to surface and refute, not avoid.

The rule must be reasoned from structure (a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex is n−2 triangles), not merely curve-fitted to 3, 4, 5 sides; a pattern that happens to fit the given cases but wasn't reasoned may not generalise.

A static triangulation diagram or a pre-filled table is a useful reference for showing the decomposition, but by itself it does not let the learner conjecture a rule and test it on a new case — pair any static display with an actual conjecture-and-check task.

An interactive explorer or a well-designed quiz (deriving the rule, finding a far term, and selecting the case that disproves a false rule) can each be used during teaching, not only for assessment; choose by what the learner needs to do, not by assuming one medium alone can teach generalisation.

3D representation is unlikely to be needed here because polygon angle sums, linear sequences and operation properties are flat/symbolic; it may add handling load rather than insight for this specific content. This is a scoped judgement about this topic, not a universal or verified claim about 3D.
Area models/algebra tiles are an optional representation whose fit is strongest for simple binomial products; do not present them as a verified or required method for the cubic cancelling pattern.

Self-audit of the examples used: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon (6−2)×180° = 720°, decagon (10−2)×180° = 1440° — all consistent with (n−2)×180°. The n×180 distractor gives pentagon 900° and hexagon 1080°, correctly shown as wrong. Sequence 5,9,13,17 has rule 4n+1: 4th term 4×4+1 = 17 ✓, 20th term 81, 100th term 401 — consistent.

The legacy 'possible'/'poor' fit entries carried universal-sounding claims (a tap-to-reveal 'cannot' let the child conjecture; 'open talk gives nothing to test'; '3D adds load, not insight'). These have been softened to scoped, qualified observations with stated affordances/limits in the constraints; catalog fit rankings and quiz-step vocabulary were removed.

The operation-property example was tightened to 'any whole number m divided by n can be written as the fraction m/n'; the exact source wording ('dividing by n always gives a denominator of n') was looser and reviewers may wish to confirm the intended statement.

The original source listed an algebra-tile/area-model representation for operation-property generalisations and for the (x−1)(x+1)… cancelling pattern; the applicability of area models to the polynomial-factoring (cubic) example is plausible but not established by the cited sources and is now scoped as optional and reviewable.

topic.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule; identify apparent features of the pattern not explicit in the rule and explain informally why they occur
evidence: Given 'start at 1, add 3', generate terms and notice they alternate odd/even
Given a shape pattern, predict the next three terms and describe the rule

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told 'start at 3 and multiply by 2 each time', can they write out the pattern — 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 — and spot any interesting features in how it grows?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; generate a number or shape pattern from a given rule; identify features NOT explicit in the rule and explain informally why they occur.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5–Y6 'generate and describe linear number sequences'; reasoning about pattern features.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.5 — 'generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms … and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate.'
• Operational details — two intertwined skills: GENERATE (apply a term-to-term rule accurately) and NOTICE-AND-EXPLAIN (spot an emergent feature — alternating odd/even, all even, a repeating units digit — and justify it from the rule's structure). The emphasis, as with times-table patterns, is on the informal EXPLANATION ('add 3 flips parity each time because 3 is odd'), moving from spotting to reasoning. Shape patterns (growing sequences) connect the term number to a count, seeding the position-to-term (nth-term) idea. Use a T-table (term number vs value) and concrete/pictorial growing patterns.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): generate terms from a rule and continue a shape pattern. Tier B (age 9–10): notice an emergent feature (alternating odd/even; always even) and describe it. Tier C (age 10): explain informally WHY the feature must continue, from the rule's structure.
bestPractices: Separate and then connect the two demands: generate accurately, THEN look for a feature the rule didn't state and explain it.
Press for informal explanation grounded in structure ('adding an odd number flips odd↔even'), not restatement of the observation.
Use a T-table (term number vs value) so emergent features and the position-to-value link become visible.
Include growing SHAPE patterns (dots/tiles) alongside number patterns, connecting the picture to the count and seeding nth-term thinking.
Encourage prediction ('what will the 10th term be? will it be odd or even?') and verification.
keyRepresentations: T-table (term number ↔ value) — exposing emergent features
Growing shape/dot pattern — term number as a count
Number line / hundred square — visualising step patterns and parity
Colour-coded terms (odd/even) to make features pop
commonMisconceptions: Applying the rule inconsistently or miscounting steps when generating terms.
'Explaining' a feature by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Assuming a short-run feature always holds without justification (over-generalising).
Confusing the term-to-term rule with a position-to-term rule.
Not distinguishing the starting number's role from the step's role in an emergent feature.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: generate a number or shape pattern from a given rule, then notice a feature the rule did NOT state (alternating odd/even, all-even, a repeating units-digit cycle) and explain informally WHY it must continue from the rule's structure. The teaching goal is to move from spotting a feature to justifying it (e.g. 'adding an odd number flips parity each time'), using a term-number vs value table and growing shape pictures to seed position-to-term thinking.

activities.title: Generate, then colour by parity to spot a hidden feature
feedback: If the differences between your terms aren't all the same (e.g. 1, 4, 7, 9, 12), you added to the wrong term or changed the step partway — mark the +3 jump between every pair to enforce a constant step.

If, when asked what else you notice, you only repeat 'it goes up by 3', look specifically at the last digits (1, 4, 7, 0, 3, 6, 9, 2 …) or at the odd/even pattern — those are features the rule didn't tell you.
Check your 10th term by continuing the sequence; the colour pattern should let you predict its parity before you compute it.
activities.rationale: Separating accurate generation from feature-noticing, and using a term-number vs value table plus parity colouring, makes emergent features and the position-to-value link visible, as the standard requires.
sourceClaims: Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
T-tables and growing shape patterns support generate-and-explain reasoning and seed position-to-term thinking.
learnerActions: Take the rule 'start at 1, add 3' and write the first eight terms: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22.
Mark each 'add 3' jump between consecutive terms (on a number line or by an arrow) so the step stays constant.
Colour or mark each term as odd or even and describe what you notice about the sequence of colours.
Record each term in a table with two columns: term number (1st, 2nd, 3rd …) and value, so emergent features line up next to their positions.
Predict whether the 10th term will be odd or even, then generate it and check.
activities.intendedInsight: A rule states a step, but the generated sequence can show a feature the rule never mentioned — here the terms strictly alternate odd, even, odd, even — and a table or parity colouring makes that feature visible.

activities.title: Explain WHY the feature must continue
feedback: If you say a feature 'just is' (e.g. 'the terms are all even because they just are'), push for the reason: even + even = even, so an even start plus an even step stays even.
If you predict odd terms will appear in 'start at 2, add 4', generate a few terms to test the prediction, then reason that adding an even step preserves evenness.
A correct explanation points to the step being odd or even (and, for an all-even or all-odd pattern, to the starting number's parity too) — not simply to the terms you happened to list.
activities.rationale: The objective's heart is informal explanation grounded in structure; pressing past restatement to a parity/digit reason is what distinguishes procedural term-cranking from the intended reasoning.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.5 requires generating a pattern from a rule, identifying features not explicit in the rule, and explaining them informally (e.g. why +3 from 1 alternates odd/even).
Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
learnerActions: For 'start at 1, add 3', explain why the odd/even labels keep alternating: adding 3 (an odd number) flips parity every single time, so the alternation must continue forever, not just for the terms you wrote.
For 'start at 2, add 4', predict before writing whether every term will be even, then justify: starting even and adding an even number keeps the result even, because even + even = even.
State a prediction for a step of 2 instead of 3 and explain how the parity pattern would differ (adding an even number leaves parity unchanged).
Give a structural reason, not just a restatement: say WHY it happens from the rule, not merely THAT it happens.
activities.intendedInsight: An emergent feature can be justified from the structure of the rule: an odd step makes the terms alternate (and the starting number fixes which parity the alternation begins with), while an even step keeps every term the same parity (and the start fixes that parity). So the feature must hold for all terms, not just the observed ones.

activities.title: Vary the step to discover the roles of start and step
feedback: If changing only the step also seems to change which parity the terms begin from, check that you really held the starting number fixed — change one thing at a time.

If you can't yet say why the colour locks for an even step, connect it back to the fact that adding an even number never changes parity (even + even = even, odd + even = odd), while adding an odd number flips parity.
activities.rationale: Changing one variable at a time (step, then start) lets learners experimentally separate the two ingredients of the rule and avoid confusing the term-to-term rule with the position-to-term rule.
learnerActions: Keep the start fixed and change the step from 3 (odd) to 4 (even); generate both sequences and compare the parity colouring — alternating for the odd step, locked for the even step.
Now keep the step fixed and change the starting number; notice which feature changes (which parity the terms begin with) and which stays the same (whether they alternate).

Articulate the two distinct roles you discovered: the step's parity decides whether the terms alternate (odd step) or stay a single fixed parity (even step); the start fixes which parity the sequence begins with — the one it stays on for an even step, or the one it starts the alternation with for an odd step.
Test a prediction before computing: for a new rule, say what the hidden feature will be and why, then generate terms to confirm.
activities.intendedInsight: The starting number and the step play different roles in an emergent feature; experimenting by changing one at a time isolates each role.

activities.title: Growing shape patterns and position-to-term
feedback: If you predict later stages only by drawing every one, try using the stage number and the per-step growth to jump ahead, then check by drawing.
If your described rule doesn't reproduce the next term, re-count one stage and recompute the change between stages (it may be constant, or it may itself grow in a pattern, as in square arrangements).
activities.rationale: Including growing shape patterns alongside number patterns connects the picture to the count and seeds nth-term reasoning, as recommended for this objective.
sourceClaims: T-tables and growing shape patterns support generate-and-explain reasoning and seed position-to-term thinking.
Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
learnerActions: Continue a growing dot or tile pattern by predicting the next three terms and describing the rule in words.
Count the dots/tiles in each stage and record stage number next to the count in a two-column table.
Link the stage (term) number to its count, and predict a later stage's count, explaining how you used the position rather than drawing every stage.
Notice any hidden feature in the counts (e.g. always even, or a repeating units digit) and explain it from how the shape grows each step.
activities.intendedInsight: Growing shape patterns connect the term number to a count, seeding position-to-term (nth-term) thinking and giving a concrete picture of an emergent numeric feature.

activities.title: Pattern-detective discussion: justify the feature aloud
feedback: For 'would 30 ever appear from start 1, add 3?': the terms are 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, … and each one is one more than a multiple of 3 (it leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3). 30 is itself a multiple of 3 (remainder 0), so it can never appear. Notice that 30 is even and ends in 0 — and terms ending in 0, like 10, 40, 70, do occur — so parity and the units digit alone do NOT settle it; you have to reason from the step, that every term stays one more than a multiple of 3.

If your answer repeats the observation, the detective should ask 'but WHY will that keep happening?' until you name the structural cause — such as the step's parity, the even+even rule, or (for questions like whether 30 appears) the remainder every term leaves when divided by the step.
activities.rationale: A questioning dialogue that refuses restatement and demands a structural reason is well matched to the informal-explanation demand and pairs naturally with a generated sequence and table the learner has built.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.5 requires generating a pattern from a rule, identifying features not explicit in the rule, and explaining them informally (e.g. why +3 from 1 alternates odd/even).
learnerActions: With a partner or adult playing a 'pattern detective', state a feature you noticed and be ready to defend it.
The detective accepts the feature ONLY when you give a structural reason for why it continues (e.g. 'adding an odd number flips parity each time'), not when you restate the observation.

Answer probing questions such as: 'Besides adding 3, what pattern do you see in the numbers?', 'Why do the terms of start-at-2-add-4 stay even?', 'If you start at 1 and add 3, would 30 ever appear — how can you tell?', and 'What changes if the step is 2 instead of 3?'
Revise your explanation if it's only a restatement until it names the structural cause.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining informally means giving a reason rooted in the rule's structure that shows a feature must persist, not merely reporting what you saw.

constraints: The aim is both skills together: generate accurately AND notice-then-explain a feature not stated by the rule; listing correct terms alone does not meet the objective.
Explanation must be structural (why the feature must continue), not a restatement of the observation.
Distinguish the term-to-term rule (the step) from a position-to-term rule; keep the starting number's role separate from the step's role.

Response formats that only ask a learner to pick the correct explanation from options can check whether they can distinguish a reason from a restatement, but do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing and voicing their own structural justification; use them to assess, and pair with tasks where the learner generates terms and explains in their own words.

A static exemplar table and growing-shape picture can anchor the idea and reveal a feature, but cannot let the learner vary the rule and test how emergent features change; provide that experimentation separately.

Interactive examples (auto-colouring terms by parity, a table filling in as terms are generated, a reveal-the-reason prompt, changing the step to compare) are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required tools.
Do not over-generalise a short-run observation; require justification before accepting that a feature always holds.

When judging whether a target value can appear in an arithmetic sequence, reason from the step's effect on remainders/divisibility, not from parity or units digit alone, since those surface features can be insufficient (e.g. 30 is even and ends in 0 yet cannot appear in 1, 4, 7, 10, …).

State the role of the step precisely: an odd step makes terms alternate in parity while an even step holds a single parity; the start only sets which parity begins the sequence, so avoid saying terms 'settle/lock to a value' in the alternating (odd-step) case.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'poor-fit' note claimed a third dimension 'adds no explanatory power'; this has been dropped as a catalog-preference statement rather than retained as a universal claim. Number/shape sequences are naturally represented in a table and growing picture, but no necessity claim is asserted.
Two of three cited sources were marked unverified in the source row (CCSS 4.OA.5 wording and NCETM guidance); treat their claims as legacy-stated, not independently re-checked here.

Self-audit of worked values: 'start 1, add 3' gives 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22 (units digits cycle 1,4,7,0,3,6,9,2); 'start 2, add 4' gives all even terms; the '30' probe is determinate (terms ≡1 mod 3, 30 ≡0 mod 3, so 30 never appears). These were checked and are consistent.

Correction applied this pass: the 'Explain WHY' intendedInsight and the 'Vary the step' action/feedback said the start sets a 'value they lock to / settle on', which is false for the alternating odd-step case; reworded so locking is attributed only to even steps and the start is described as setting the starting parity. The sourceClaims on the 'Vary the step' activity were set to [] because no source claim directly supports the controlled-variation principle.

pedagogy.summary: Systematic listing enumerates all combinations of two categories (e.g. 3 starters × 4 mains) so that none is missed and none repeated, by working in a fixed order: hold the first choice constant, run through every second choice, then move on. Organising the combinations into a table or tree makes completeness checkable, and reveals that the total equals the PRODUCT of the number of options in each category (3 × 4 = 12) — an early foundation of multiplicative counting.
bestPractices: Model a fixed order — hold starter 1 and pair it with every main in turn, then starter 2, and so on — rather than listing haphazardly
Record in a two-way grid or tree so gaps and repeats are visible and completeness can be argued
Ask 'how do you know you've found them all?' and value the answer 'I worked systematically'
Draw out that the total = rows × columns = the product of the options (3 × 4), not the sum (3 + 4)
Start from sorting/ordering the child's random attempts to expose what is missing, then move to generating in order
Offer the tree diagram as an alternative systematic structure to the grid

Recording the combinations in a two-way grid or tree makes completeness arguable and reveals that the total equals the PRODUCT of the options in each category (3 × 4 = 12), not their sum (3 + 4 = 7). activities.title: Pair and light the grid: building every meal in order
feedback: If the predicted total was 7, point out: each of the 3 starters makes 4 meals, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4 = 12; the count is the grid's area (rows × columns = 3 × 4), whereas 3 + 4 just adds the two side counts and does not count the meals.

If the list is unordered with gaps or repeats, prompt: 'How do you know you've found them all?' and guide to the answer 'I worked systematically' — hold one category fixed and run through the other fully before changing it.

If only the diagonal (S1M1, S2M2, S3M3) was produced, note that both choices changed at once; show that a full ROW must be filled — fix starter 1 and vary the main across all four before moving to starter 2.
When the grid is complete and ordered, affirm that completeness can now be argued from the system itself, and that the whole row-by-row fill makes 3 × 4 = 12 visible as the grid's area.
activities.rationale: Starting from the learner's own random attempts and then sorting them exposes what is missing, motivating the move to systematic generation; a two-way grid makes completeness checkable and surfaces the product structure directly. A 'predict first' step confronts the add-versus-multiply error before building.
sourceClaims: Children first find all possibilities in a random way and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting their attempts exposes the gaps and teaches them to generate systematically, because having a system ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Start with 3 starters and 4 mains and first PREDICT how many different meals you think are possible before listing any — write down your prediction and say whether you think it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.

Begin by pairing starters and mains in any order you like, recording each meal you make in a two-way grid (starters down the side as rows, mains across the top as columns) by marking the matching cell.
Look at the grid: check whether random pairing has left scattered marked cells with empty gaps, or whether you tried to mark any meal twice. Ask yourself: have I found them all? Can I be sure?
Now switch to a fixed order: hold starter 1 and pair it with every main in turn (filling a whole ROW), then starter 2's row, then starter 3's row, until every cell is marked with no gaps.
Count the completed grid as rows × columns = 3 × 4 = 12, and compare this with your earlier prediction.
Explain how you know you have found every meal, and why the total is 3 × 4 rather than 3 + 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Working in a fixed order — fix one choice, run through every option of the other — guarantees no combination is missed or repeated, and the complete set fills a grid whose total is rows × columns, the product of the options.

activities.title: The tree-diagram route to the same complete set
feedback: If a starter branch is missing a sub-branch, point out that every starter must be paired with every main, so each branch sprouts all 4 mains.
If the child counts branches by adding (3 + 4), reconnect to the grid: 3 starters each with 4 mains is 3 × 4 = 12 end-points.
activities.rationale: Offering the tree as an alternative systematic structure to the grid gives a second representation of the same completeness-and-product idea; when every starter branch is given a sub-branch for every main, the tree ensures no options are left out. Whether it transfers better than the grid is not established, so both are offered as equivalent structures.
sourceClaims: Children first find all possibilities in a random way and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting their attempts exposes the gaps and teaches them to generate systematically, because having a system ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Draw a tree: one branch for each starter, then from each starter branch draw a sub-branch for every main.
Read each complete path from left to right as one meal (e.g. starter 1 → main 3).
Count the end-points of the tree and check it matches the grid total of 12.
Explain why each starter branch must sprout the same 4 sub-branches, so the total is 3 lots of 4 = 3 × 4.
activities.intendedInsight: A tree diagram is a second systematic structure that enumerates the same complete set; the repeated identical sub-branching is the product 3 × 4 made visible a different way.

activities.title: Check and extend: how many if a category grows?
feedback: If the total is given as 7, revisit the row-by-row fill: 3 rows of 4 is 3 × 4 = 12; the additive answer counts the individual options (starters plus mains), not the combinations.
If extending to a 4th starter yields an added rather than multiplied answer, prompt: one more starter adds one more full row of 4 mains, so 4 rows of 4 = 4 × 4 = 16.
If a missing combination is overlooked, ask which starter still needs pairing with which main — the empty grid cell names it.
activities.rationale: A short set of targeted checks (count with the common additive answer of 7 against the correct 12, a missing-combination fill, and a transfer prediction) probes product-versus-sum reasoning and completeness; such checks verify the skill but do not themselves build the systematic method, so they follow the building activities.
learnerActions: Answer 'How many meals are there altogether?' and justify whether it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.
Fill in a deliberately missing combination given a partly-completed grid or list.
Predict, WITHOUT listing them all, how many meals there would be if the café added a 4th starter (4 × 4 = 16), explaining your reasoning from the product structure.
Match each listed meal to its grid cell to confirm the set is complete and non-repeating.
activities.intendedInsight: The product structure lets you predict the count when a category grows without enumerating every case, confirming the skill transfers beyond the original numbers.

constraints: A completed grid or tree with reveal-on-tap can SHOW the organised set and the product, but if the learner does not build it or test completeness themselves, the systematic search and the product structure are presented rather than discovered — use it as a worked example, not as the main learning activity.

Recognition or matching checks (e.g. selecting the total, filling one missing combination) verify the skill but do not elicit the learner's own systematic enumeration method; keep an open construction task where the learner generates and orders the combinations themselves.
The structure here is inherently a flat two-dimensional grid or tree; a third spatial dimension is not needed and can obscure the rows × columns count.

A role-play dialogue may discuss the systematic method, but on its own it does not require the learner to generate and order the combinations themselves; if used, pair it with actual listing and grid-building so the learner produces the enumeration.

The additive error (3 + 4 = 7) must be confronted directly, ideally by a predict-before-building step and by reading the total as the grid's area (rows × columns), not merely noted as a possible slip.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 3 × 4 = 12 is correct and 3 + 4 = 7 is the common additive wrong answer to be avoided as the true total; 4 × 4 = 16 for the 4-starter extension is correct. No erroneous alternatives were carried into learner questions.

The 'grid's area' framing is accurate because each cell is exactly one combination, so rows × columns counts the meals; the earlier 'not the perimeter' wording was corrected because 3 + 4 = 7 is not the grid's perimeter and the contrast should be area versus the sum of the side counts.

Source citations support the general teaching principles (systematic generation; Year 6 enumeration objective) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive build, of the predict-first step, or of the tree versus grid; no claim of tested effectiveness is made. The DfE objective claim establishes the topic only and was not used as an activity sourceClaim where it did not support the specific teaching principle.

responseLevels.gap: Lists a few combinations at random with gaps or repeats; cannot say whether the list is complete; gives the total by adding or by guessing.
responseLevels.full: Enumerates all combinations by holding one category fixed and running through the other in order, records them so completeness is evident, justifies 'all of them' by the system, and gives the total as the product 3 × 4 = 12 explaining why — transferring to predict the count when a category grows.
responseLevels.partial: Lists many combinations and senses there is a full set, but works unsystematically (misses or repeats) or cannot justify completeness, and/or finds the total by counting one-by-one rather than as 3 × 4 — has combinations but not the systematic and multiplicative structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A café offers 3 different starters and 4 different mains. List every possible meal of one starter and one main, and show me how you know you have listed them all. Then tell me how many meals there are altogether, and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child working systematically holds one category fixed and runs through the other, produces all 12 in order, and gives the total as 3 × 4 = 12 explaining the product; a child listing haphazardly misses or repeats meals, cannot justify completeness, and often predicts the total by ADDING (3 + 4 = 7). Both the 'how do you know you've got them all?' question and the total separate systematic, multiplicative reasoning from random listing.
